I wish to remind the right hon. the Premier of the inquiry I made yesterday in respect to the Hindus in Vancouver harbour, and of his promise that the Minister of the Interior would make a statement in regard to that matter to-day. I hope the minister's statement will be more full and frank than that with which we have been favoured so far.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not think I made
any distinct promise. I said:
It is my belief that the reports are very largely exaggerations. The Minister of the Interior has not reported to me in regard to the matter, as I think he would have done if anything unusual occurred. I will direct his attention to the inquiry of the hon. member.

Would my right hon.
friend road a little further?

Mr. Oliver: Would the minister, instead of restricting himself to saying that the newspapers are not correct, say exactly what the position is ?
Mr. Borden: Yes.

I have just had placed in my hands the following memorandum from the Superintendent of Immigration:
The ship arrived at Victoria, B.C., on the 21st ultimo with 376 Hindus aboard, but without any bill of health. Arrangements were made with the public health authorities to pass quarantine and the ship proceeded to Vancouver, where in accordance with instructions issued

by the Dominion immigration agent, she anchored in the harbour about half a mile off shore. The medical and civil examinations have been in progress since that date. Counsel for the department called attention to the necessity of holding a board of inquiry, sitting on each individual case. This necessitates considerable delay. The examinations are being conducted on board ship, rather than on shore: first, because of our lack of facilities on shore, and further, to prevent unnecessary communication between the Hindus resident in Canada and those who are now applying for admission, and further to prevent escapes.
In the medical examination 90 of the Hindus have been rejected, while at least 4 have been landed as returning to Canada after having acquired domicile in this country. The examination is proceeding and all those who can comply with the regulations will be admitted.
The allegation that Hindus are starving from lack of food is a gross exaggeration, according to reports received from the Dominion Immigration agent at Vancouver. Yesterday I wired our agent to see that passengers do not suffer from hunger. Reports to hand this morning indicate that an offer was made yesterday to the charterer of the vessel, Gurdit Singh, to place provisions aboard and it was proposed to supply 2 tons of flour, 300 lbs. of rice, fruit and other articles, but the representatives of the Hindus refused, unless in addition to the flour, rice, fruit, etc., they were given ginger, cabbage, purified butter, milk, 50 live sheep or goats, 100 live fowl, 200 boxes of cigarettes, red pepper, spices, crates of eggs, etc. The department has offered an arrangement by which the charterer of the ship (who claims to have 1,500 tons of coal for sale) can unload his cargo, but this has been refused. The hunger strike, which has been so widely advertised, is said to be only apparent, as information secured from the ship's officers shows that Hindus are eating food at night and that food is available to meet the present requirements.
I am not particularlyinterested, nor do I think the country is, as to whether these Hindus live on fish or fowl.

Or red
herring.

What I am interested in knowing is whether or not the Government is enforcing the Order in Council passed some time ago which absolutely excludes white people from the coast ports. If it [DOT]is being enforced I do not see why there should be this extraordinary delay in passing upon the applications of these Hindus for entry. If it had been a shipload of white artisans a decision would have been reached long ago. I would also like to know whether legal proceedings have been taken, and if that is the cause of what seems to be the unwarrantable delay of the department in dealing with this matter?

I can only say that the Order in Council is being enforced
against the Hindus just as it would be against any other class of people. As the hon. gentleman knows, these men have a right, in common with every other person seeking access to Canada, to demand a board of inquiry. The examination is proceeding, but necessarily involves considerable delay, because many of the Hindus are not conversant with the English language, and interpreters and counsel have had to be engaged. A separate inquiry is held in the case of each individual, and that involves considerable delay. Those Hindus are endeavouring to prove that they are not labourers in some instances, and if one provision of our Immigration Act is not sufficient to exclude them, possibly another provision may be sufficient. Of course, we cannot take charge of the vessel and send these people back without holding an inquiry. All we can do is to prevent them landing until each individual case has been inquired into, and that will take some time.

I saw it mentioned in the papers that while this vessel was lying at anchor a shipload of Chinese were admitted into British Columbia. If this Order in Council is effective only against white men and Hindus, and not effective against Chinamen, and if it is in accordance with the law as it stands, I wish to repeat the suggestion I made before that while the House is in session means should be taken to alter the law so that that anomaly shall not be continued.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Government Orders.

I wish to
call attention to a matter which affects the privileges of the House as well as the privileges of a member, and myself in particular. I refer to a motion that was made on the 16th of March requiring the production of certain papers. This matter has been brought to the attention of the House on more than one occasion in the hope that
495t

the Minister of Customs (Mr. J. D. Reid) would see the propriety of complying with the order that was made. The minister is above any individual member of the House, or perhaps he thinks he is, but the House is above him.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member desires to enter into a discussion regarding this matter it would be out of order at this stage.

I submit, Your Honour, that I may bring up anything affecting the privileges of the House at any time. This is a matter that affects the privileges of the House, as I shall prove to you toy quoting an authority that you will recognize.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Then I take it that the hon. member proposes to make a motion in connection with this?

Just so. As I stated, ministers are obliged to obey the orders of the House. It is laid down in Bourinot, page 364, that:
If a person neglects or refuses to furnish a return or frames it so as to mislead, it is a breach of privilege.
Then Bourinot says, at page 371:
The right of a member to obtain information from the Government within the limits previously described is so undoubted that it seems almost beyond the power of a minister to keep the practice within narrower bounds and thereby save much public money.
There is a declaration that the right of a member to obtain information within certain limits is undoubted. The limits are described on pages 364-367. My hon. friend the Minister of Customs will search these pages in vain to find any justification for his conduct. But that is not all. On page 367 Bourinot says:
It is the duty of the minister submitting papers not complete to give the reason why the order could not be more fully complied with and then the House will judge whether the reasons are satisfactory and act accordingly.
I can quote oases where the minister has claimed the right to withhold papers but I cannot find any case that is on all fours with this case because the eases I find in the authorities are those where there was at ah events a semblance of compliance and not a refusal to produce the papers. In this case there is not the slightest pretense or excuse for the refusal to comply with the order. If there were any such excuse that excuse should not be kept from us. The order of the House having been made, the

duty of the minister is to comply with it. Either the motion was, or was not, in order and if it was not in order it was the right and privilege of the minister to take exception to it at the time. Let me quote from a statement made toy the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie on March 17, 1874:
Every member was entitled to information when he asked it; it was never refused by any Government. The hon. Minister of Public Works had no right to assume a member was asking for anything improper. That doctrine would enable a minister to use his majority, when he saw fit, on a matter of opinion, to refuse information.
The papers which were referred to on that occasion were:
Copies of all papers, letters, and correspondence relating to the dismissal or replacement of William Robertson, clerk of works and inspector under the contract for building the penitentiary, Dorchester, N.B.
Sir Charles Tupper did not claim that the papers could be withheld but he rather objected to the production of the papers because of the unimportance of the matter under consideration. But the principle was laid down that the production of these papers' was the right of the member. Let me quote what Sir John Macdonald said as recorded at page 494 of 'Hansard' of that year:
The practice in Canada had been so long in existence that, unless by arrangement made by both sides of the House for more strict supervision, they could not well resist the motion; the practice had prevailed so long that a refusal would be regarded as an attempt to stifle inquiry.
Then he went on to say:
Still, he thought hon. gentlemen would admit that indiscriminate motions for papers already returned constitute a crying evil.
But he lays it down that it is the right and privilege of the member to move for papers and to get them. I made my motion on the 16th March and you will see how the minister has neglected to comply with it. Here is the return:
Sessional Papers, No. 77 T.

On the face of the return it is absolutely incomplete. Does any hon. member of the House suppose that a collector of customs would be appointed without a recommendation being made by somebody? Where is the recommendation on which this appointment was made? Where is the authority for the appointment? As a matter of fact there was a recommendation made and there was -more correspondence in connection with the matter. The appointment of a collector of customs is a public matter. It is a matter in which the public at large, as well as the people of Antigonish, are interested inasmuch as the people pay that man's salary. Any recommendations that were made respecting the collector of customs ought to be brought down in compliance with the order. I happen to know that there was a recommendation made in this ease. The appointment that was made was a very unpopular one. The Conservative party in Antigonish were dissatisfied with it.
Senator Girroir, who had charge of the patronage after the former collector of customs died, refused to take the responsibility of making a recommendation, and he suggested that delegates be appointed from each district in the county, to meet and decide who should be given the collec-torship. These delegates met and deliberated and several names came before them, and, on the casting vote of the president of the Conservative Association, John Boyd was recommended. But Senator Girroir refused to endorse this recommendation, and notwithstanding that he had previously assured the delegates that he would abide by the decision of the convention, he afterwards made a recommendation by telegram to the Commissioner of Customs asking that Mr. W. C. Chisholm of Heatherton should be appointed. Then the president of the Conservative Association, speaking for the association, sent a letter to the Minister of Customs in which he described all the facts, stating that Senator Girroir had first declined to assume responsibility himself, and then asked for a convention to make the recommendation, that he had refused to carry out the recommendation of the convention when it was made, although he had agreed in writing that he would abide by the decision of the convention, whatever it might be. The president of the Conservative Association enclosed this written agreement of Senator Girroir to the Minister of Customs, The Minister of Customs will not get up on the floor of the House now and deny that he got that letter. I know, as a matter of fact, that he did. I do not know it from Dr. W. F. McKinnon, president of the Conservative Association, personally, as that very respectable and trustworthy gentleman did not take me into his confidence. But the whole Conservative party in the country were indignant, and Dr. McKinnon had no hesitation in telling the party what he had done, and the contents of the letter are within the knowledge of the people of that district, although they are denied to this Parliament. It is a matter of small concern to me, whether that letter is brought down or not; I am placing the matter before -the House in order to vindicate the rights of Parliament. Hon. gentlemen on the other -side must remember that they may be in the same position themselves some day. Is a minister forsooth, to tell this House of Commons that he is the sole judge as to whether or not he -shall bring down a document? I repeat that the Minister of Customs received this letter-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member is exceeding the rule in going into the full details of the history of this matter. The question is, whether the Government should bring down these papers as a matter of the right of every member of Parliament to get

information, and the remarks of the hon. member would be more appropriate if he would address himself to that feature.

I am explaining to
the House what is the nature of the document, so that the House may understand that it was neither private, nor confidential, nor personal. I say that when that document was sent to. the Minister of Customs it was not intended to be regarded in any such light. There is nothing to justify the minister in withholding this document, because all the surrounding circumstances show that it was not intended to he either private or confidential, but on the contrary that it was a public protest made by the Conservative Association of Antigonish through their president. If there is any information required of this, I may mention the fact that the Prime Minster himself was advised of the letter sent to the Minister of Customs, and as the minister from Nova Scotia he was asked to cause action to be delayed until such time as the representations made on behalf of the Conservative party and the people of Antigonish could be fairly considered. Cushing lays down the reasons for refusal to produce papers in Parliament. His first statement is, that it must be on account of state reasons, and as we all can appreciate there could be no state reasons for refusing to bring down this document. Cushing gives another reason to the effect that papers should not be brought down, if it is contrary to public policy to bring them down, and nobody can say it would be against public policy to bring them down in this case. Then Cushing says: Documents that are private and confidential are not brought down, but as I have shown these are neither private nor confidential. I submit that no minister is justified in saying that he has the right to determine whether a thing is private or not. If a document is marked ' private ' or if the circumstances are such as to indicate it is private, he has the right to refuse to bring papers down, but if he can hold back such a letter as that which I have referred to, then the minister, if he so determines, could withhold all information from this House. The authority lays down:
It is the duty of a minister submitting papers not complete to give the reason why the order is not complied with, and then the House will judge whether the reasons are satisfactory and act accordingly. .
I ask that the minister now disclose to the House, in accordance with parlia-

mentary practice, why he withholds this information and why he brings down a report that is incomplete, and after he has told these reasons it will be time for the House to act accordingly.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman send up his motion ?
I move that the House adjourn.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is not the motion that should be presented to the House, under the rule.
I claim that I can bring the matter up any time as a matter of privilege, and without a motion, substantive or otherwise.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think it is properly a matter of privilege; but when the hon. member told me he intended to conclude with a motion, I did not expect it would be a motion for the adjournment of the House provided for in another rule, which says that in the event of something of urgent importance being brought to the attention of the House, a request should be made for leave to move the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing it, and then, if the House agrees, it may be discussed. But, this is a different thing.

When the minister has stated the reasons why he has not brought down the information it will be for the House to determine how to act. I purpose moving a resolution then, if necessary, or if you wish I move now:
That it is the duty of the Minister of Customs to comply with the order of the House of March 16, 1914, relating to the appointment of the collector of customs at Antigonish.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My non. friend has taken up a good deal of time in discussing a matter that does not seem to be of very great importance. There is no objection to his motion passing. Of course, it is the duty of the minister to comply with the order of the House. As a matter of fact, he has already complied, we understand. The question of compliance with such orders of the House has been under discussion many times in Parliament in my experience, but I have never heard, up to the present time, any suggestion that documents essentially private in their nature and coming from persons exercising patronage must necessarily be brought down and laid on the table. As a matter of fact, the question of the confidential character of

such communication must always be in the judgment of ministers of the Crown.
Does the right hon. gentleman say that these are confidential documents?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I say that any documents not brought down are, in the judgment of the minister, private and confidential. The House is not concerned with them; they are not appointments, or anything in the nature of appointments to the public service. The responsibility for such appointments is on the minister, and the minister may listen to recommendations from one source or from another, but it does not necessarily follow that the files of the House shall be encumbered with documents to which possibly no attention may have been paid. I have known extreme cases while I was in opposition. I remember at the moment, one arising about 1898. I moved for one particular document, being a report from an officer of the Government in respect of a claim against the Govern-ernment.	If I	remember correctly,it was	made	by Mr.	Shanley.
I moved in this House for that report, giving its date and a full description, and the order passed the House. Yet the document was not brought down, because Mr. Blair, who was then Minister of Railways and Canals, said that it was not in the public interest that it should be brought down-notwithstanding that the House had ordered it- and it has never been brought down from that day to this. These matters must always be in the judgment of the ministers of the Crown, and in this respect the Government take full responsibility for the course they have taken in this matter.

The case has been very -well set forth by my hon. friend, from Antigonish (Mr. Chisholm). A motion was made for certain documents concerning an appointment made in the Customs, and amongst other papers called for were the recommendations upon which the appointment was made. If the recommendations under which the appointment was made were confidential, nobody would pretend that they should be brought down. But my hon. friend asserts, and has reason to believe, that there were such documents that were not of a confidential nature. No exception was taken by the minister, and the order passed that all papers, including recommendations, should be brought down. That is the order of the House, and the order must be complied with. I admit that
the Prime Minister is right when he says that a minister must exercise judgment in this matter. But we know that, according to the doctrine laid down on the other side, in a debate concluding only yesterday, the minister is bound to exercise good judgment, and if he does not exercise good judgment he is liable to the consequences. If the minister tells us that the recommendations on which the appointment is based are of a confidential nature, he is not obliged to bring them down. But it is for him to say whether or not they are of that nature. My hon. friend from Antigonish is right in this: the Minister of Customs made an appointment. I am sure he did not know personally the gentleman who was appointed-somebody suggested his name. It may have been perfectly open; the recommendation may have come from the merchants of the town of Antigonish, from the Board of Trade, or from any person; it may have been of a confidential nature. If the papers are of a confidential nature, he is not bound to bring them down, but if they are not he is bound to bring them down. My right hon. friend has no objection to the passing of the motion. It is for my hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid) to say whether he has complied with the order of the House or not. If they are confidential, there is nothing more to be done; but if not my hon. friend from Antigonish (Mr. Chisholm) will have to consider what further steps he will take. He will certainly have some recourse.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Customs):
speechtext: I remember the order in question. I gave instructions that all the official papers in my department relating to the matter should be brought down, and they were brought down. If there is any other correspondence in connection with this matter, it was considered by me to be private and confidential. The right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) knows that while he was in the Government similar orders were made by the House for papers in connection with appointments to office, and never in one case, I believe, did the right hon. gentleman bring down private correspondence in connection with these matters. But, so far as this appointment is concerned, I may say that I discussed it verbally with certain parties.
How about the telegram?

There may be other telegrams or letters considered by me as private, and

I certainly would not, on any terms, bring down papers of a private and confidential nature.
How about the recommendation of the Conservative Association decided at a general meeting?

If there are any such documents, I do not consider them public documents. I assume full responsibility for any appointments made in the Department of Customs, and I also reserve the right to get any information I feel to be necessary in order to decide who should be appointed to any office in my department that may be vacant.

The doctrine is a new one, that the House is not entitled to know the recommendations for appointment to office. I have never known even the present Administration to refuse this information. I can show dozens of recommendations to office incorporated in returns that I have in my desk. If any person had written to the minister a private and confidential letter stating that a certain person was not a fit and proper person to be appointed to office, that might fairly be withheld. But communications, such as those referred to by my hon. friend from Antigonish, are different from that. One of these arises out of a convention of the whole Conservative party of Antigonish; surely there was nothing private about that; it is well known in Antigonish and throughout that part of Nova Scotia. It is absurd that the minister should say that a document which has come into his hands arising out of a meeting of that kind in regard to an appointment to office is a private document. If such a document can be refused to the House, it is open to any department to refuse any information of this character.
It is certainly a new doctrine-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: This is not a substantive motion; therefore the hon. gentleman would not have the right to reply except with consent of the House.

With the permission of the House, I desire to make one statement. The Minister of Customs certainly lays down a new doctrine when he says that it is unnecessary to bring down recommendations to position or office. The Postmaster General, who is a good lawyer, brought down a return recently, and in the file there was a letter written by Senator

Girroir to the Postmaster General, marked private and confidential. The letter made complaints against the postmaster at Harbour au Bouche, and asked that another person be appointed in his stead. On the same file there is a letter from the Postmaster General to Senator Girroir, stating that the recommendation on which me change was made was this same letter which was marked private and confidential, but, inasmuch as it was marked private and confidential, he wished to take the liberty of putting it on the file and using it as a public document if there were no objection. The Postmaster General recognizes that it is necessary to have the recommendation of some responsible party, and he gets permission of the person who writes a private and confidential letter to use it as a public document; yet the Minister of Customs says there is no necessity of bringing down such recommendations.
Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My right hon. friend will remember that in 1864 delegates of the governments of the Maritime provinces gathered together in convention in Charlottetown to consider the question of maritime union, that delegates of the united provinces of Upper and Lower Canada came to that convention and that they postponed their deliberations in order to enter into a larger convention which would take into consideration the foundation of the present Confederation. The people of Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, are desirous of commemorating that historical event, which is invested with certain significance. When the application was made for the grant we were informed that the cost of the celebration would amount to a very considerable figure; the balance is to be raised by private subscription.

speechtext:
A press conference of
various leading journalists from all parts of the world is proposed; I am not absolutely sure that it will take place this year.
I understand that it will take place this year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
When representations
were made to us with regard to the matter, we expressed some doubt as to whether .the organization of a conference on so large a scale could be successfully undertaken within the time limited, and we must have some assurance as to the representative character of the conference before arranging to pay any portion of this sum.

Anything, of
course, which will advertise Canada we should readily agree to, and I imagine that this organization will be of that character. So far as that is concerned, I have no objection, but I should like to know who are promoting this organization.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: A committee of Canadian journalists, of which Sir John Willison is, I think, the chairman. I am not able at the moment to say who the other members are.
Perhaps the hon. member for Edmonton knows something about it.
I have had no communications to lead me to understand that the conference will take place this year, but as I am not following the proceedings very closely I am not an authority.

The reason why I say
that the congress will meet this year is because in a monthly circular issued by the Imperial Press I observed an announcement that the conference would meet this year. The article dealing with the matter was accompanied by photographs of Sir John Willison, Mr. Dafoe of the Winnipeg Free Press, and other noted Canadian journalists. It seems that there is a central committee in London acting in co-operation with the Canadian committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The Canadian Peace Centenary Association was organized on June 4, 1912, for the purpose of organizing the celebration in Canada of the centenary of the signing of the treaty of Ghent.
The project of holding this celebration had been broached first in the United States and afterwards in Great Britain. So far as is known, the first person to make the suggestion publicly was the Hon. Mackenzie King, who mentioned the proposal at a ceremony held at Harvard University in 1910. The American Committee was organized soon after and has been in operation for about four years. The British Committee was the next- to be formed, and the Canadian Association came into being as the result of the interest taken -in this country in the proposals put forward.
The president of the Canadian Peace Centenary Association is Sir Edmund Walker, and the executive committee comprises:	S. Baker, M.P., Hon. Justice
L. P. Brodeur, LL.D., George Burn, Esq., Hon. G. A. Clare, M.P., Hon. Senator Raoul Dandurand, K.C., LL.D., Lieut.-Col. F. D. Farquhar, D.S.O., W. M. German, Esq., M.P., Hon. Senator Robert Jaffray, Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, C.M.G., M.A., Ph.. D., Hon. Sir Alex. Lacoste, K.C., D.C.L., LL.D., Travers Lewis, Esq., K.C., C. A. Magrath, Esq., Chief Justice, The Hon. Sir Wililam Mulock, K.C., K.C.M.G., LL.D., Hon. G. H. Perley, M.P., Sir Joseph Pope, K.O.M.G.,	C.V.O.,	I.S.O,, Elias
Rogers, Esq., Albert Sevigny, Esq., M.P., Hon. Clifford Sifton, K.C., Mrs. F. H. Torrington, J. C. Walsh, Esq., W. G. Weichel, Esq., M.P., Major 'C. F. Hamilton, and C. Cambie, Esq. The members of the association now number upwards of one thousand, and great interest has been shown in the proposal by the churches, the press, public bodies, and the general public.
In May, 1913, delegates from the association attended an international conference

held in New York between delegations from the three bodies concerned in the movement. At this conference the general lines of a celebration were agreed upon. The proposals fall under four headings:
1.	The erection of visible monuments, as enduring memorials of the Century of Peace.
2.	The holding of appropriate public demonstrations.
3.	The carrying on of an educational propaganda in the schools, designed to impress upon the pupils the benefits of peace.
4.	The holding of suitable religious exercises.
On June 5, 1913, following the holding of this conference, in reply to Mr. W. M. German, M.P., I made a statement which included the following paragraph:
While the Canadian Peace Centenary Association is an unofficial hody, the Government strongly sympathizes with and approves of its object and purpose of promoting good will and peace between the nations of the world. The Government Is disposed to give favourable consideration to a grant such as that mentioned in the question in case similar action should be taken in other countries.
la. June, 1913, the association secured the services of Mr. E. H. Scammell as organizing secretary. Mr. Scammell in the eleven months which have elapsed since his appointment has visited every province in the Dominion, has addressed a great number of meeting, and has carried on an effective work of organization. At present arrangements are on foot for the holding of upwards of 60 local celebrations, and new places constantly are being added to the list. Work also is being prosecuted along other lines of the proposals. Offices have been taken in the Hope Chambers.
On February 20 last, in reply to Mr. W. G. Weichel, M.P., J made a statement in which, after recalling my utterances of June 5, 1912, and stating that the Government still adhered to them, I noted the work done by the association and the similar bodies ini Great Britain and the United States and said:
I am informed that a Bill appropriating a sum of money for the purposes of the celebration is now pending in the United States Congress. In answer to my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Weichel), I beg to say that, subject to the approval of His Royal Highness the Governor General, it is the purpose of the Government to insert in the Supplementary Estimates to be introduced this session the sum of $25,000 for the purpose of defraying the preliminary expenditures incurred in the work of organization.

This vote is requested in accordance with this statement and by reason of the considerations which I have briefly set forth.
Amount required to meet expenses of Technical Board appointed to consider questions relating to the level of the lake of the Woods, $10,000.
'Mr. OLIVER: In what connection were questions raised with reference to the waters of the Jake of the Woods?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There have been very
difficult questions, which have been referred to the International Joint Commission.
It was in that connection that questions were raised, and this evidence was taken for that purpose?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have a memorandum
here which explains the matter fully:
With the concurrence of the Governments of Canada and the United States,
12 noon several questions affecting the levels of the lake of the Woods have been referred to the International Joint Commission under article IX of the Boundary Waters Treaty for investigation and report. As the question of levels affects the various departments of the service, it was deemed advisable to name a board, composed of various members of the departments concerned, to look into all the various intricacies of the reference, and to prepare a report for the Government so that its policy regarding the matter might be framed upon sound investigation. The board is composed of Honourable J. D. Hazen, chairman ; S. J. Chapleau, Department of Public Works; D. H. Fraser, Department of Marine and Fisheries; W. J. Stewart, Department of the Naval Service; J. B. Challies, Department of the Interior, and H. G. Acres, representing the Hydro-Electric Commission of Ontario.
None of these officers received any extras for serving on this board, but the amount of $10,000 is placed there to cover small investigations, surveys and clerical assistance required in the collection of data now in the hands of the various departments.

Is there a
similar board in the United States?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not aware that there is. My hon. friend will remember that in the United States all such matters are under the charge of the engineering staff o: the army, and in that way they have a much better organization for the purpose of protecting their country's interests than* we have in this country. For that reason we think it desirable in the public interest that this board should be created.

I understand that the city of Winnipeg applied to the Joint Waterways Commission for power to take the water from the lake of the Woods. Has the

Waterways Commission decided that they have jurisdiction in that matter, and, if so, have they given the city permission?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand that the decision was entirely satisfactory to counsel representing the interests of the Dominion of Canada, but what the precise nature of the decision was I could not tell my hon. friend at the moment. I will have an inquiry made and give my hon. friend the information on concurrence.

The jurisdiction of the
commission was admitted, then?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There are various incidents in connection with the matter which I cannot now quite recall. First of all, a certain contention was put forward on behalf of the province of Ontario, and, if I remember correctly, it was afterwards modified. All I can say with certainty at the moment is that the question did come in some form or other before the commission at a meeting held in Washington some time ago. I remember distinctly being informed by counsel who represented Canada on that occasion that the decision of the commission then arrived at was entirely satisfactory from our point of view.

The point of
danger is not to the city of Winnipeg, which, I believe, has the right to use the waters of the lake of the Woods. The point of danger is from applications which have been made by some American cities which wished to divert the waters flowing north and turn them eastwards towards lake Superior. That is the difficulty. For my part I think the board which is presided over by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has very valuable work in hand and can do a great service to the country. I would like to know if the board has been at work already, and whether it has made a report.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The board was organized only a short time ago. In the first place, they had a great deal of work to do collecting and collating information upon this matter which is scattered about in the different departments. That work is now going on, but no report has been made up to the present time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It was thought necessary, I think about a year ago, to make some inquiry as to Government records scattered around in the various buildings in the city of Ottawa under the jurisdiction of the various departments. A commission was appointed, and it has bestowed a very large amount of time and labour on the work, with results that are very useful indeed. I shall be most happy to show to any hon. gentleman the report which they have submitted; it is very well got up indeed. Their work resulted in the discovery of very valuable documents scattered in out-of-the-way places. For instance, a number of old and important documents relating to the early days of the Militia Department were found in an old stable or shed on Sparks street; and similar illustrations could be given.
My right hon. friend should have the report printed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Of course, the whole report is very voluminous, and I think there are also eight or ten volumes of typewritten matter as an appendix to the report. I think I laid the main report on the table of the House some time ago. Under the circumstances it was thought to be only proper to make this small allowance, which is really only a slight remuneration for the labour which was imposed on the commissioners in the discharge of their duties.
I think the report should be printed and indexed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I shall be very glad to take into consideration what my hon. friend from Rouville suggests as to the printing of the report. I hardly think it will be necessary to print the appendix.
Royal Northwest Mounted Police-Contingencies-Travelling expenses, $600.
I saw a statement in the papers that it was intended to send an expedition into the far North to take measures in connection with the death of explorers Street and Caldwell of Ottawa. Is that a fact?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is not undertaken as a punitive expedition, but for the purpose of making the tribes in the North understand that the safety of white men must be assured. A good deal of information was collected as to the incident to which my hon. friend refers. The particular tribes in that part of the country do not know anything about our laws and customs. I think it is a custom among them having the

force of law that under certain circumstances and conditions every man is at liberty to take the law into his own hands and to redress his private wrongs. In that respect they are in a condition of civilization which our ancestors were in perhaps two or three thousand years ago. They have not been brought very much in touch with white people. The difficulty of sending an expedition into that country for {purposes of punishment might be very considerable and result in the end in a very much worse condition of affairs than prevails at the present time. I took the opportunity of consulting my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition in regard to this matter, because I knew he had had a great deal of experience in similar cases, and the conclusion at which I arrived and which was based upon the report of the comptroller and other officers of the Northwest Mounted Police was one which I understood he approved of. He thought it desirable that there should be an expedition sent there for the purposes to which I have alluded. It is to be hoped that the result of the expedition will tend to improve the conditions amongst the Indians, and it is felt that better results will follow this expedition than an expedition of a more aggressive character.
When is the expedition to go ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think it has started already.
What is the strength of it ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have not that information but I will get it for my hon. friend.

These Indians of the North are mostly, if not altogether, Esquimaux, and they are of a very peaceful and kindly nature. The time is perhaps remote when there will be any considerable settlement in their country, but at the same time I think we should gradually extend our jurisdiction to those northern waters and regions. There is nothing of which we can avail ourselves in these lands at the present time, but they are full of coal and perhaps other minerals, and at a perhaps not distant period these lands are bound to become very valuable. It is of the greatest importance that the jurisdiction of the Canadian people and of the Government should be asserted quietly as it is proposed to do at the present time. The force that is to be sent to that country is a very limited one and, from the character of the officers, is a very good one. It is well to let the

Indians know that the white man and the Canadian Government are their friends and protectors.

While the Main Estimates of the Mounted Police were under consideration I drew the attention of the right [DOT]hon. gentleman to the fact that the criminal conditions existing in the prairie provinces to-day is more pronounced than that which has prevailed in past years. In the papers that came the other day there was a case mentioned in which a justice of the peace was shot to death by two or three outlaws or miscreants without any reasonable provocation, and to-day the countryside is alarmed and the people are out trying to find the assassins. I do not wish to lay any blame upon anybody, but I want to emphasize the point that conditions tending towards lawlessness are more extreme to-day than they were some years ago and that the increase of population has not tended to the decrease of the lawless element but rather has tended to the increase of it. I think it only right that the Government should have that point emphasized to them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The comptroller has sent to me from time to time reports respecting certain items that have appeared in the public press. The reports which he has sent to me I have always regarded as fairly satisfactory. I have not them under my hand at the present moment, but if my hon. friend would like to see them I shall have them in concurrence and communicate them to the House. I think that, as far as the performance of their duties by the Royal Northwest Mounted Police is concerned, the reports which I will then communicate will be found thoroughly satisfactory.
Pensions-To increase the pension of Mrs. Margaret Johnson Brooke, from 75 cents to $1.25 per diem, $182.50.
What is this?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mrs. Margaret Johnson
Brooke is the widow of the late Staff Sergeant Brooke, who was drowned while on duty in 1903. She was granted a pension of 75 cents per diem, representing one-half of the pay of her deceased husband. Unfortunately, the shock of his sudden death upset her reason; she became insane and is confined in the asylum at Verdun, Quebec. The cost of her maintenance at Verdun is 1.25 per diem and up to the time of the inquest, a short time ago, the balance was paid by her father. She has no relations who are in a position to support her and.

under the distressing circumstances of the case, she being unable to take care of herself, it is proposed to increase the pension to $1.25 per diem to permit her to remain in the asylum.

While we are discussing this question of pensions, may I bring to the attention of my right hon. friend a case which is not similar but which is germane to the present one in a sense. I have been asked by many persons, amongst them friends of the Administration, to bring it this year again to the attention of the Government. I refer to the case of Madame Hector Fabre, widow of the late Canadian commissioner in Paris. My right hon. friend is aware that Mr. Fabre was the first Canadian commissioner appointed by the Government in France some thirty years ago. He had been a very prominent public man in Canada, especially as a writer. He was, in his day and generation, the most eminent writer in the French language in Canada. When he was appointed commissioner, although our trade with France was somewhat limited, and although the immigration from France was very small, Mr. Fabre, thanks to his many relations in France, thanks to his connections with the journalistic and intellectual world, contributed immensely towards the better knowledge acquired by the French people of Canada and her resources. At that time Mr. Fabre received from this Government a very small salary-I think something like $3,000 or $4,000 a year. As our country grew in importance and the number of people visiting France increased, every year, he was obliged not only to give all his time to his office but to draw upon his own private resources in order to maintain the dignity of his position. He died three years ago and it was my sad privilege to attend his funeral when I was in Paris. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) knows that he was beloved by all those who came near him. He was extremely popular in France and certainly by his writings he advertised Canada and secured for us most precious friendships. I would not say that he left his widow penniless, but he left her in poor circumstances and she cannot maintain, with her private resources, her station in life, Sir, what has happened since the death of Mr. Fabre? The Government has appointed Senator Roy as commissioner in France and his salary as commissioner has quite properly been raised from $4,000 to $12,000. Every one acknowledges that the Canadian commissioner in Paris, as in London, or in 313
any of the large European capitals, but especially in London and Paris, should receive a decent salary so as to enable him to do justice to his position and to represent worthily his country. During Mr. Fabre's lifetime, he had the title of Canadian Commissioner, but he received a very paltry salary although he had all the responsibility of representing this country in one of the greatest capitals of the world. His family has forwarded to me, and I think to. the Minister of Justice and others as well, certain documents which show that during his tenure of office, he, being a most generous and kind-hearted man, continually took his own money to pay for the maintenance of Canadians who unfortunately were stranded in Paris, and to send them back home to Canada. This occurred in quite a number of instances. I wish to read the following affidavits:
I, the undersigned, Eug&ne Meiffre, being duly sworn, depose and say:
That I am in business at Ballu street in Paris, France.
That during twenty years I have known intimately Mr. Hector Fabre, in his lifetime Commissioner General for Canada and France, and I had the greatest friendship for this gentle soul who has conquered the respect of all Canadians in France.
That Mr. Fabre continually helped Canadians in Paris and often spoke to me of these poor beings whom he pitied so much, and to whom he felt in duty bound to give money, although it was never returned to him.
That Mr. Fabre's charities were well known, .and according to him he must have spent from 2,500-3,500 francs a year either to help Canadians or to send them home.
(Signed) EugSne Meiffre.
Sworn before me in Paris on the 19th March, 1913.
Edgar Attwell Smith, British ViceConsul, Paris.
I, the undersigned, EugSne Capdeviel, do depose and say:
That during eleven years I was the office boy of the late Mr. H. Fabre, and had to pay the rent and expenses of the Canadian Government offices.
That Mr. Fabre always requested me to buy the steamship and railway tickets of the persons whom he sent back to Canada, and that I have given several times upon orders from Mr. Fabre to Canadians in need, sums ranging from 15 francs to a few hundreds of francs.
That I accounted for the expenses to Mr. Fabre, who checked them but never took any note thereof.
That the said charges and costs must, in my opinion, have exceeded 3,000 francs a year, and that over and above the said charges I may state that every year Mr. Fabre spent 15,000 francs for office expenses, divided as follows:

Lighting	 700

Repairs and up-keep of office ..	500

That it is through me that the said sums were paid for about ten years, with the exception of the wages of the three employees, which I fixed at a minimum sum, and which sum must have been larger.
That I know that Mr. Fabre received 12,852 francs a year as indemnity for above expenses, and in view of the fact that Mr. Fabre spent for office expenses.alone 15,064 francs, he paid out of his own pocket 2,222 francs a year for office expenses. There is no doubt in my mind that Mr. Fabre spent out of his own pocket 3,000 francs a year in charities and about 2,200 francs for extra office expenses.
