Sworn and acknowledged before me at the British Consulate in Paris on 22nd April, 1913.
Edgar Attwell Smith,
British Vice-Consul, Paris.
I, the undersigned, Count le Moyne de Mar-tigny, being duly sworn, do depose and say:
That during twenty years I have been the daily companion of the late Mr. Hector Fabre, Commissioner General for Canada and France;
That during the whole of that period I was familiar with his many charities to distressed Canadians who came daily to ask him for assistance, which he never refused.
That Mr. Fabre spent yearly out of his own pocket 3,000-4,000 francs to help Canadians or send them home. I remember a Canadian family named Pate, composed of the wife and three children whom he assisted during one year and sent home. In that case alone he spent nearly 3,000 francs.
That his time and money were always at the disposal of Canadians and his acts of charity are well known to his friends and to all those who had relations with him.
That Mr. Fabre spent altogether at least 3,000 francs a year in charities or to send Canadians home, and that the said charities must have cost him during those twenty years over 60,000 francs.
(Signed) Count Le Moyne de Martigny.
Sworn before me at the British Consulate in Paris on the 28th March, 1913.
Edgar Attwell Smith,
British Vice-Consul, Paris.
Sir, again I say, let the Government remember that the late Mr. Fabre, during his lifetime, and out of his modest income, rendered most valuable services to Canada. He, with his brilliant pen advertised our country throughout France as no other writer could. He died with hardly any savings, and, although his widow is not penniless, yet she is too poor to maintain in Paris where she resides her station in life. On behalf of the family,' a family of patriots, and the many friends and admirers of this distinguished Canadian, I would ask my

right hon. friend to consider this case and to see whether or not a sum of say $10,000 might be granted to recoup his widow for the many large sums of money the late Mr. Fabre spent during his term of office, first, in assisting distressed Canadians in France, and, second, in representing worthily the country he loved so much.
Mr. BORDEN; I realize that the salary Mr. Fabre received during the period he occupied his important position was very inadequate, not only when viewed from certain standards, but also in consideration of the many calls made upon him then, and of the expense which he was obliged to incur in connection with his position. The Government also realizes that Mr. Fabre was a very distinguished man, and that in many ways he rendered good service to his country. My hon. friend will, however, realize that there are a great many other claims of a somewhat similar character that are constantly pressed upon the Government, and that it is very important in the public interest that no principle should be established which would involve embarrassment in the future. The principle, that because the salary of a public servant during his term of office was small, we should make provision for those who survive him, is a pretty broad principle to lay down. Personally, on the general consideration of this claim, I viewed it with a great deal of sympathy, as I am sure all the members of the Government did. This question and a great many similar and analogous questions are now under the consideration of a subcommittee of the Privy Council for the purpose of ascertaining whether or not there is any solid foundation upon which we can proceed in reference to any one or more of them. At the moment I cannot add anything to [DOT]that.
The hon. member alluded to the salary that Mr. Roy draws. When we came into power we found Mr. Roy drawing a certain salary; but, in addition, he had been accorded the privilege of acting as an official director of some company which, as I understand it, was established to make investments in Canada. He was also receiving a salary from the province of Quebec as a representative of that province. We arrived at the conclusion, after certain representations made from different quarters, that it was inadvisable that Mr. Roy should occupy an official posi-sion such as he did in connection with a company, as other companies desiring also

to make investments in Canada might consider that the company with which Mr. Roy was connected enjoyed special advantage by reason of that connection. We thought it inadvisable, also, that the representative of the Dominion a6 a whole in Paris should also represent a particular province. On the other hand, we had no desire to dispense with the services of Mr. Roy, and we desired to deal with his case in a considerate manner. We took up the question by correspondence and verbal conversation, and, in order to give him practically the same status which he had enjoyed under the arrangements theretofore existing, we decided to increase his salary to $12,000. Of course, he han to relinquish the considerable remuneration he received from the company, and also the salary he enjoyed from the province of Quebec.

The sub-committee, I
understand, will examine all these claims?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: A very large number of claims, not all exactly analogous to this, but all more or less connected with the subject.

My right hon. friend
will see that this one comes under that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This, undoubtedly, will
be placed before the committee.
Miscellaneous-To compensate William Tate of Prince Albert, for expenses incurred by him in connection with illness contracted while serving with Prince Albert volunteers during the rebellion of 1885, $1,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Tate was engaged
in scoutng in the rebellion of 1885, and after the engagement at Duck lake, on the 26th of March of that year he was sent with despatches to Prince Albert, and received injuries through the long cold ride, having to remain in the saddle for fifteen hours. After eleven years suffering from hemorrhoids he was operated on in the Royal Victoria Hospital, Montreal, incurring expenses of over $1,000. It is proposed to grant him this indemnity therefor. I have very full particulars here with regard to this case. On the occasion referred to, after being in the saddle for fifteen hours on this ride, he had to receive medical attendance. He continued to suffer for many years afterwards, and eventually, on the advice of Dr. Bain he went to Montreal and was operated on toy Dr. Bell. Between March, 1885, and the date of the operation, he had to employ outside labour to do the work of his farm which he was unable 3134
to perform owing to his injury. His expenditure for medical attendance, medicine, surgical treatment and the employment of men on his farm amounted in the aggregate to at least $1,500 We have thought it reasonable to bring in a vote to compensate him to the extent of $1,000, which is the amount expended for medical attendance. The comptroller is of the opinion that the sum of $1,500 claimed is well within the limit of the loss which Mr. Tate sustained in actual cash, if we include the labour he has had to employ on his farm. That, however, is excluded, and Mr. Tate is willing to accept $1,000. I think that under the late Administration a somewhat smaller amount was proposed, but Mr. Tate did not agree to accept it. The matter has been standing for some years upon the question of the amount of compensation-not with regard to the principle of compensation-for the injuries which he sustained.

I am not finding fault with the decision of the Government to pay this claim except in this way: We are aware that a large number of similar claims arose out of the 1885 rebellion, as must necessarily arise under any such conditions, and it seems invidious that Mr. Tate's claim should be paid and others ignored. As I say, I do not find fault with the payment, and I presume this claim is a just one; but it certainly is a matter for remark and gives rise to very serious consideration, that one claim out of a large number which have been standing for so many years should be paid, and only one should be paid. I do not wish to minimize the services rendered by Mr. Tate, but these services were no greater than those rendered by many other men at the same time and under quite as difficult circumstances. I do not wish to put the matter in a nasty way, but I confess that it looks as if this claim were being paid as a matter of political pull rather than as a matter of merit.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not aware of any political pull about it. I have not heard a word of politics upon the subject, unless possibly it is to be found in a report of the late comptroller of the Northwest Mounted Police. The only suggestion coming from any person connected with active political life is contained in the following:
Mr. T. O. Davis, M.P. for Saskatchewan, assures the undersigned that of his persona] knowledge Tate has suffered continuously since the rebellion and apart from indirect losses

through physical incapacity, has been put to very considerable expense for medical and surgical relief; and that although he has no reason to doubt that the $1,500 claimed by Tate is well within the limit of his actual loss and expenditure, he is satisfied that he would accept a smaller amount, say $500 in settlement of his claim.
It turned out that that was incorrect; it was offered to him, but he thought it inadequate.
What is the date of that report?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The date of writing is not given here, but the report must have been made some years ago. It was under consideration by the late Administration. I am informed that the Government of my right hon. friend Sir Wilfrid Laurier were willing to pay $500, but Mr. Tate was not willing to accept it. This is not at all for services; it is merely a partial compensation for actual losses sustained through the injury which Mr. Tate received during that rebellion.

I have not a distinct recollection - of this matter, but I am sure that my hon. friend is opening the door somewhat wider than he thinks when he goes into this kind of claim. After the rebellion of 1885, the Government of that day, under Sir John A. Macdonald, settled all the claims which arose from that rebellion. From that day to this there has been a constant pressure upon all governments from certain parties claiming that they should receive compensation which was not given to them at that time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have not heard of any of these claims since the Northwest Mounted Police came under my administration; if I do hear of them, I shall endeavour to give my best consideration to them. So far as this payment is concerned, it does not even go as far as the principle of a pension; it is merely compensation for actual injury sustained.
Transcontinental railway-operation of line from Moncton to L6vis, $175,000.

The right hon. leader
of the Opposition asked for any correspondence in connection, with the purchase of the railway from the viaduct to St. Malo shops. I stated to him that the negotiations had taken place verbally and had been carried on by myself during the absence of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, and by the minister himself since his return. The price asked by
I Mr. Borden.]
the Canadian Northern Railway Company was very much more than either I or the minister thought the line was worth, and the result was that the Minister of Railways and Canals had decided to expropriate the line and have the prices fixed by the Exchequer Court. That the minister verbally advised Major Leonard, the commissioner, to do so is quite evident from a letter which was addressed to the minister, dated June 4, as follows:
Dear Mr. Cochrane:
In pursuance of our conversation of the 2nd instant, I am filing to-day plans for the expropriation of the five miles of the above line between Cap Rouge and St. Malo, and will notify the Canadian Northern to that effect.
The chief engineer is instructed to get this line into repair at the earliest possible date, so that the Grand Trunk Pacific can obtain coal during this season of navigation at the Quebec harbour and store it on our line for the necessary operation west from Quebec during the coming winter.
Yours sincerely,
(Sgd) R. W. Leonard.
In the absence of the Minister of Railways and Canals, I replied as follows:
Dear Mr. Leonard:
In Mr. Cochrane's absence I have yours of the 4th instant in which you state that you are filing plans for the expropriation of the five miles of the Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia railway between Cap Rouge and St. Malo.
I think it would be better to file expropriation plans in order that the title may be obtained.	*
However, for your information, I may say that this portion of the road has been purchased. Mr. Cochrane, the regular minister, has agreed to purchase the road from the Canadian Northern for the amount of one hundred and seventy-five thousand dollars.
As soon as you are able to have the title proved, I wish you would see that the purchase is completed on the basis of the amount suggested above.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd) J. D. Reid,
Acting Minister of Railways and Canals.
That is about the way the matter stands. This Canadian Northern hne passes the St. Malo shops and, by arrangement with the Canadian Pacific railway for the joint use of the terminals in the city of Quebec, which extend to the St. Malo shops, we shall have access not only to the union station but to all parts of the Quebec harbour around the Louise basin. In addition to that, after the tunnel is completed, we shall be in a position to run through trains direct to the Canadian Pacific railway station in Quebec. With the new station which is being constructed on the Champlain market with the ferry crossing the river and with the acquisition of this line, there is no doubt

that we shall be able to take through freight and passengers to all parts of the city of Quebec, thus carrying out everything that was promised the city of Quebec, except the tunnel, and that will be completed as soon as possible.

Very far from it. My hon. friend will have a lot to do before he establishes communication round the harbour at Quebec by means of this line. He will have a line of railway five miles in length from Cap Rouge to the shops at St. Malo, but he will have to make an arrangement with the Canadian Pacific railway to get communication between the shops at St. Malo and the union station. Last year the Minister of Railways told us that he was contemplating buying this Canadian Northern line to establish communication with the shops at St. Malo, and it has taken him one year to come -to any kind of conclusion in the matter. We find that an agremeent has been made, but no papers have been signed; I suppose that next year the contract will be entered into. But even when this is done he will not have completed arrangements to get all round the city. He will have arranged for the taking of his lame ducks for repair from the tracks at Cap Rouge; but he will have five miles of railway communicating wdth the shops at St. Malo, but, if 1 am correctly informed, that will not take.him to the shops; he will still have more to do. But even supposing it does, What communication will he have between the shops and the union station? That will have to be arranged with the Canadian Pacific railway. Then again, there is no communication between the Champlain market station and the line of the Canadian Pacific railway. We were told last year by the minister that this was to be attended to by the harbour commissioner. What in the world the harbour commissioner would have to do with building a line of railway there is more than I can understand. When we come to discuss that matter I shall have to have an explanation from my hon. friend as to what has been done since last year in that regard. The fact is that in this matter there has been negligence unpardonable. My hon. friend has to-day told us that he has made arrangements for the acquisition of that line, but he has not laid the contracts before the House, although a year ago he told us that negotiations were in progress, it has taken him twelve months to arrive at an agreement wnich is not yet reduced to writing or embodied in a contract. What are the terms of this arrangement? The Canadian Northern railway have sold this line, but I am told they must have reserved some rights on it.
No rights.

What becomes lof their line, then? They have a railway system running from Ottawa to Quebec, and for that main line they must have access to the river front, to the bridge; otherwise? it would be of little use to them. Does my hon. friend say that the Canadian Northern railway have surrendered their line and have reserved no rights whatever on it? They go towards the bridge by that line, they have sold five miles of it and my hon. friend says they have reserved no running rights over it.

The right hon. gentleman
knows that that piece of line of the Canadian Northern railway has not been used for months; it is not part of their main line into Quebec at all.

What did
they build it for?
They built it, as I understand, to get material around at the time.

The Canadian Northern railway is the owner of the Quebec Central railway and it is part of their business, and it is common sense that they should have a line of communication from one line to the other. It is part of their system, part of the very Canadian Northern railway system to which we have given $45,000,000. The Canadian Northern railway have built a line of railway from this city of Ottawa to Quebec, and the two lines must be connected. My hon. friend tells me that the Canadian Northern railway have reserved no running rights at all over that line. If they have not done so they are not as good business men as I had supposed them to be.
And they are not treating the junior partner right.

No, they are
not treating the junior partner right. My hon. friend had better inquire further and he will find that there must be some condition attached to the sale of that five miles of railway.
So far as I am aware, there are no conditions, and they have not been using this line for months.
They built it for fun?
No, they did not build it for fun; but at the time they built it they used it to get heavy material around to the bridge.

Did not they get a
Dominion subsidy for it as well?
I cannot speak as to that.

My hon. friend might be ready at three o'clock to answer these questions: How much will it take to put the line into, good operating condition? What is the weight of rails and condition of the road? Is it the intention of the Government to build a lock at what is known as Morton's lock on the Rideau?
That is an old story.
I understand it has been promised -within six weeks by a member of the Government. Will there be an item for it in the Supplementary Estimates?

The Estimates for this year
are all down.

I cannot find it unless
it is hidden away under some other item.
At one o'clock, the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

I would just like to say a few words with regard to an item on page 52 of the Main Estimates providing for additional facilities at Riviere du Loup at a cost of $77,600. These improvements have been under contemplation for many years. It has been proved-I think the minister must have the information in his department-that by unloading the coal at Riviere du Loup instead of at Levis as at present, the management of the Intercolonial would save in the neighbourhood of $15,000 a year. Mr. Gutelius himself admitted last year in the presence of the Riviere du Loup Board of Trade that that was a fact. More than that, he said that the Grand Trunk Pacific would also profit by it if the coal were unloaded at Riviere du Loup. If this Government ever purchases the Temiscouata railway which con-[DOT] nects with the Grand Trunk Pacific at Ed-mundston, the Grand Trunk Pacific would be able to get its coal more cheaply and quickly at Riviere du Loup than at Levis where it is unloaded at the present time. He said that as soon as the Department of Railways and Canals were ready to make this expenditure at Rivifere du Loup he would be willing to spend thousands of dollars for new facilities and machinery at 
Riviere du Loup. On page 70 of the Main Estimates there is an item providing for wharf improvements at Rivifere du Loup at a cost of $50,000. Could the minister tell me if any arrangement has been made between his department and the Department of Public Works to proceed with this work at once ? When we were discussing the Estimates last session, I asked Mr. Rogers when he expected to call for tenders, and he told me they would be called for at once; but I do not think it has yet been done. I think the time has arrived when we should have a definite statement from the minister as to whether any such agreement has been made with the Public Works Department, and as to when it is intended to proceed with the work.

I have discussed this matter several times with the Minister of Public Works, and I understand that he intends to proceed with the work as early as possible. I agree with every word the hon. member has said. I have before me a statement showing that if the coal were unloaded at Riviere du Loup it would save thirty cents a ton or $15,000 per annum.
I shall urge the Minister of Public Works to go on with the work as early as possible in order that we may save this $15,000 per annum.

Will the minister
assure me that he will urge this upon the Minister of Public Works?
I have just stated thaf so far as the Department of Railways and Canals is concerned we will urge the Minister of Public Works to proceed with this work at the earliest possible moment.

As the Minister of Public Works is not present, I may say that this matter has been under the con-, sideration of the two departments for a long time. The difficulty has been that the work was to be done by the two departments jointly. Some time last year, during the early fall, I think, I succeeded in getting representatives of the two departments to go down on the spot to meet Mr. Gutelius, whom I asked to take a personal interest in this matter. Mr. Tremblay represented the Department of Public Works. Mr. Gutelius presented a report, and as'a result of bringing the two departments together I can say definitely that the work will be proceeded with before long. As my hon. friend says, it is a matter of interest not only to the locality but to both the Intercolonial and the Grand Trunk

Pacific. My hon. friend has just heard what the acting Minister of Railways has said, and I have myself made efforts in that direction for some time. Pressure of business, however, has prevented the work from being started up to the present. I remember the Minister of Public Works making the statement last year to which my hon. friend has referred. I shall be very happy to see this work undertaken, not only in the interests of Riviere du Loup, which is very much in need of it, but in the interests of the country at large.
Is it the intention of the Government to bring a railway subsidy Bill down this session?
Not so far as I am aware.
Has the Government been approached for a subsidy by the railway running from Midland to Montreal, and is it the intention of the Government to treat that railway as others have been treated?

I remember some persons connected with that railway interviewing me with reference to subsidy. I gave them the same answer that I would have given to anybody else. As far as that railway company is concerned, there have been no promises made, nor will we make any promises. Whenever subsidies are taken up, if subsidies are to be granted next session to any railway companies, all applications will be taken up and considered, and we will then have to consider whether we will grant that or any other company a subsidy.
That means, I understand, that the company, on its own demand or request, will be treated in the same way as any other company coming before the Government?
That company, like any other company, will be treated on its merits.
On the same footing?
They are all on the same footing, and they will all be treated on their merits.
I would like to ask the minister if there is any reason why it should not be treated as being on the same footing?

As far as I am concerned, there is no reason why that or any other railway should not be treated on the same basis, but if the hon. gentleman wants an
answer as to whether it is the intention to give that railway a subsidy-
No, I do not.
There is no promise, and they will all be treated alike on their merits.
Is there any reason why this company should not be treated as any other company?

Every company will be
treated on its merits and in no other way.
I promised my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition that I would submit a plan of the station at the Champlain market, Quebec. The plan is on the table and I have called it to the attention of my right hon. friend. With reference to the line of railway from Viaduct to St. Malo, five or eight miles in length, he asked me what it would cost to put it in a condition equal to that of the Transcontinental railway. In discussing the purchase of this railway, the Canadian Northern railway said that it would not take more than $2,000 per mile. I am informed by the chief engineer of the Transcontinental railway that it might take between $20,000 and $30,000 to put it in perfect condition, or in the same condition as the Transcontinental railway.
Do not believe it.

Has the Government any intention of being represented before the Privy Council in London in the appeal of the several railways against the judgment which has-been rendered in the court of appeal in Montreal regarding the injunction with reference to the work being done on the line of the Central railway between Ste. Agathe and St. Adolphe in the county of Argenteuil? Has the Hon. Mr. Perley, who left yesterday for London, received instructions to that effect?
I am sorry that I cannot give the hon. gentleman an answer.
I ask the question only. I do not want to put the Government in an embarrassing position, but I would be glad to get the answer as soon as possible.
I really know nothing about the matter, as this is the first I have heard of it.

I understand that the
Government has no intention of taking

action against the company, and that it will be treated as other companies are.

Is there any direct
connection between the Transcontinental and the Canadian Northern at Cap Rouge?

The line which we have purchased, and which we were discussing before the House rose, gives the Transcontinental railway, as I understand it, connection right through the city to the union station and to the harbour. We have connection over this Canadian Northern railway line with the St. Male shops, and we have access to the harbour toy reason of the fact that we have running rights over the Canadian Pacific railway in accordance with the agreement which we have made, so that we have a line right through. As far as the Canadian Northern are concerned, they have their main line between Quebec and Montreal; they do not connect directly with the bridge and they do not want that connection. If they have any freight that they wish to transfer to the Grand Trunk Pacific to go over the bridge, they will transfer it where the connections are at the city of Quebec. They are not asking to go to the bridge, and they do not require this portion of the line. Even if this short piece of line that we have acquired did not afford access to the St. Malo shops, it would be important as giving access to the union station which will be used by the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Pacific railway. Then, it is the intention to build the tunnel.
When?

I will come to that in a
moment. It is the intention to build the tunnel. The hon. gentleman knows it will take some time; it may take a year or a couple of years to complete it possibly. Is it not a good thing to have direct connection into the city of Quebec for which purpose we get this line already built? We will have, it may be within a few weeks, an entrance right into the union station and beyond to all parts of the harbour.
From Ottawa to Quebec?
Yes, and from all the other lines..

The minister is aware that the Transcontinental railway at Cap Rouge is on top of a steep hill, probably 200 feet high, and that there is no connec-

tion between the top of the hill and the Canadian Northern railway.
It is not necessary.
Is there any connection between the Transcontinental railway at Cap Rouge and the Canadian Northern railway?

The hon. member knows
that all exchanges of freight between railways are made at the terminal points. They do not stop half-way along the railway and make changes of that kind. It is at the terminal point at Quebec that the exchange will be made between the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific.

My hon. friend said
that this tunnel would be built within two years.

I did not make any such
statement; I said that this tunnel is to be built and that it might take a year or two years. No person knows what obstacles they may meet with. Does the hon. gentleman say that it is not well to have this connection right into the union station so that we can have the use of the lower side of the harbour at Quebec, and the elevator and terminals there? I think it is a splendid idea.

It is a splendid idea if you have the idea of humbugging the people of Quebec with the tunnel until after the next general election, because it will never be built. Have you an amount in the Estimates for the tunnel?
Mr. Chairman-

Answer the question,
yes or no.

Wait until I answer the first question. As far as humbugging is concerned, the hon. gentleman must agree with me when I say that during the many years he represented the eastern part of Quebec there was no one who did more humbugging than the hon. gentleman himself. Since this Government came into power we have been doing everything we could to improve the harbour of Quebec and everything connected with it.
(My hon. friend knows that the Government does not intend to build that tunnel. Is there an amount in the Estimates for the construction of the tunnel this year?

The hon. gentleman knows
that there is an appropriation of several million dollars for the Transcontinental railway, and that out of that vote the Government have power to build a tunnel or to do anything in connection with the railway.

The Government has
power to do almost anything; they have power to pay the depositors in the Farmers Bank; but what I want to know is, where is there a tittle of evidence that the Government is going to start the construction of the tunnel this year? There is nothing in the evidence to show, and it is only part of the great humbug that is being played at the expense of the people of Quebec.

I again make the statement that the tunnel can be built out of the vote for the Transcontinental railway, and that it is not necessary to have a separate item for the construction of that tunnel. That item includes the tunnel, and therefore there is an item in the Estimates for the tunnel.

What is the estimated
cost of the tunnel?
I did not make that up.
Have you any plans?
The Transcontinental Commission no doubt has plans and estimates of the cost of the tunnel, but I have not these estimates before me. I will get the information for the hon. gentleman.

Will the minister lay
on the table of the House the specifications and plans, and the approximate cost of that tunnel, and state when tenders will be called for?

I cannot say whether the
plans are yet completed, but I shall be glad to give the hon. gentleman any information that is available.

The hon. member for Rouville has made a statement on this matter to-day, simply in order to have his papers in Quebec publish it with flaring headlines, as they have been doing for the last two or three years, and it is just as well that I should straighten this matter out now. We have no Sunday newspapers in Quebec, but the remarks of the hon. member for Rouville will appear in Monday morning's Liberal newspapers, and it will be stated that the hon. member for Rouville
had told the House of Commons that the tunnel was all humbug.

You are accustomed to
being told that.

The people of Quebec were accustomed to being humbugged for the fifteen years the Liberal Government was in power, but that is not the way it is going to be now. I point out to the hon. member for Rouville that a plan has just been laid on the table of the House which shows the location of the tunnel.

But there were two
plans not very long ago.

I appeal to you, Mr. Chairman, that this discussion is out of order. We are dealing with the Canadian Northern line between Ottawa and Quebec, on a question put by the hon. member for Quebec Centre (Mr. Lachance); but the discussion has wandered off to the tunnel. The Canadian Northern passes through La-chute and Two Mountains, and I have something to say on that matter. I do not see why the Postmaster General had to get up to take the place of the acting Minister of Railways.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Postmaster General was answering a question put to him.

My hon. friend from
Two Mountains (Mr. Ethier) had better wait a moment; he will have his turn by and by. It will be seen from the plan which has just been laid on the table of the House that the location of a tunnel is shown, and, as the hon. gentleman knows, this plan comes from the Transcontinental Railway office. I am not concerned as te whether or not the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) believes that there is an attempt to humbug the people of Quebec, but I will tell him that while the people of Quebec have been humbugged in the past by the Liberal Government, I do not intend to stand by and let them be humbugged in the future. I would remind the hon. member for Rouville that the question of the tunnel was dealt with by the Hon. Mr. Cochrane as well as by the Prime Minister, who, at a banquet tendered him last fall by the citizens of Quebec of both political parties, announced that the tunnel would be built. I am not a bit worried as to whether the hon. member for Rouville thinks or does not think that is humbugging the people of Quebec; but I tell the people of Quebec from my seat on the floor of this House that faith will be kept with

the declaration made by the Prime Minister in that respect before the Citizens of Quebec. My hon. friend from Rouville is [DOT]afraid that if that tunnel is built it will not suit his party, and that his newspapers in Quebee will lose a good chance of making political capital out of the fact that the word of the Prime Minister has not been kept. But let me tell him that the declaration made by the Prime Minister has been renewed in this House this morning and this afternoon by the acting Minister of Railways, and, when the tunnel is realized, as it will be, the declaration of the hon. member for Rouville that it is all humbug will count for nothing.
I do not know whether the word ' humbug ' is parliamentary or not, but if it is-
You were the first to use it.

It will be remembered that at the first session of this Parliament the Postmaster General stated most positively-as positively as he declares this afternoon that the tunnel will be built- that there would be no Champlain Market station, and that it would be a blunder to have a station there.
I never said that.

Yesterday, however, the Postmaster General stated as positively, and with apparently as much honesty as in the first case, that that was the very place for the station. 1 believe that this tunnel is being held out merely as a bait for the people of Quebec in the next election; I believe that the Government does not intend to build that tunnel, and that it never will be built. The very best evidence of that is the very vague and mysterious answer given a moment ago by the acting Minister of Railways. It is plain that the Government does not wish to be committed to that scheme, and it will never be carried out.

The hon. member for Rouville is doing now what he is in the habit of doing: he is putting words into my mouth that I never uttered. He says that at the first session of this Parliament I declared that I was absolutely opposed to a station at Champlain market, and that a few days ago I declared that I was in favour of a station being erected there. These are not the facts, and it is no use trying to deceive the people.
What did you say yesterday?

I will tell my hon. friend once more what I did say. When we came into power there was a plan for building a large station at the Champlain market, but with no other accommodation. for the Transcontinental at Quebec.
No.
No use denying it.
I do deny it most emphatically. That was not the plan.

The hon. gentleman
may say what he likes but I have seen the plan twenty times. And the plan a3 outlined was to have only one station and that at the Champlain market. There i3 no use denying it.

I do not deny that.
But the hon. gentleman said that there was to be no other accommodation for the railway.
No other station accommodation.

That is not what the
hon. gentleman said.

Then we agree that
the only station that we were to have at Quebec was the one at the Champlain market. That is a fact, and it cannot be denied. When we came into power, we decided that the station at the Champlain market was not a proper one, that there was no place there for a proper terminal station for Quebec. I was opposed to that plan then and am opposed to it now. We discarded that plan. Other plans were made for a union station down at the Palais, and also a local and smaller station at the Champlain market. So, instead of one station as outlined by the late Government the Transcontinental will have two stations at Quebec-a large freight 'and
passenger	station at the Palais,	anda smaller	freight and	passenger	station	at	the Champlain	market.	So,what	is	the use	of the	hon.gentleman	saying I was	opposed to	the
Champlain Market plan, and am for it now. That is not the fact. I was opposed to having only one station in that small place. There is room there for a small station, but not room for the large station which the late Government intended to

put there. So we have replaced this big station with a union station at the Palais and a smaller station at the Champlain market. If that is not clear, I do not know how to make anything clear.

Some time last evening the item of the Trent Valley canal was reached. I understood that the discussion on that subject was to take place to-day. But after I left the House my hon. friend from West. Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) undertook to go into the question of the Trent Valley canal, particularly with reference to the report of the commission on the canal. This report, though dated 19th February, 1914, was placed in the hands of members of this House only during the last week of April. But I am sorry to say that in the meantime it was spread broadcast through the Conservative press of the country-as is usual in the case of such commissions nowadays-by some agency or authority unknown to me. It is used for the purpose of poisoning the public mind as to the contents of that report and the evidence on which it is based. If you search the files of the Conservative newspapers during the last week of February and the first week of March you will find some very flagrant and untrue references to the report itself. Members of the House, as I say, did not receive copies of the report until the last week of April. I was asked if I would go into the matter, and I did so. I had intended moving an amendment to the motion for Supply, but no opportunity having been given me since I took the matter up, I am quite prepared to discuss it now without moving the motion which I had intended to move, but from the same standpoint as that from which I would have discussed the matteT. The motion is as follows:
This House is of opinion that the report of the commission appointed to investigate the Trent Valley canal is partisan, unfair and misleading in many of Its findings and in others is contrary to the evidence adduced before the commissioner and should not be received by this House.
That is my estimate of the report at the present moment, founded upon a careful reading of a large portion of the evidence- I confess I have not read every line of it as it comprises some 600 or 700 pages of typewritten material. Last night my hon. friend from West Peterborough undertook to deal with that report. I had not the opportunity of hearing him, but I have had the opportunity and pleasure of reading
to-day his remarks as they appeared in ' Hansard.' It was a Royal Commission that was appointed for this investigation. The appointment was made on the 14th of October, 1912, and the commission was authorized to investigate the charges with regard to the purchase and use of explosives on the Trent Valley canal. That is the single point. Subsequently, on the 28th of November, 1912, the powers of the commissioner were enlarged, and he was authorized to carry on an investigation into the general administration of the canal and the conduct of its employees. The commissioner appointed was Mr. G. Howard Ferguson, a member of the local legislature of the province of Ontario. After some investigation-though not by any means a complete or thorough one-Mr. Ferguson placed his report on the table of the House on the 18th of February last. My hon. friend from West Peterborough last night, I think, made an effort to evade the report altogether. I do not wonder that he evaded it.
I think that after calm consideration of the findings in the report any hon. member will come to the conclusion that this House would not be justified in acting upon it. There are findings in the report which are contrary to the facts proven in the evidence; there are allusions which cast a slur upon the names of many honest citizens in the neighbourhood of Peterborough which are most unwarranted. The commissioner must have been very forgetful or very careless in regard to the evidence which he had heard, because he made findings which were unwarranted, untrue-I do not mean purposely untrue but really untrue as applied to the facts which he has found. There are one or two points in the report of the commissioner which I think the House might consider. There is no doubt that in the office system adopted in connection with the canal there were grave irregularities. In fact, there was apparently no office system at all; things were permitted to go on which should not go on under a business staff. And, in so far as the commissioner confines himself to matters of that kind I have no exception to take to his report. But he goes further-for whatever reason I know not, unless it be to blacken the record of the former Administration and uphold the record of the present Administration. If that be his reason it is an improper reason and he has fallen far short of the aim he had in mind.
Now, his first commission asked him to deal specifically with the single question of the supply of blasting powder. And the

first portion of his report, the first two or three pages deal precisely with that question. And the only irregularities he found in regard to blasting powder, if there were irregularities at all, took place under the present Conservative Administration-not a single item has been found incorrect under the former Administration. It is strange to note that no irregularity was found until the present Government exercised patronage in the appointment of a man who had not heretofore acted in connection with the supply of blasting powder. I am informed that after the general election and change of Government one Cinnamon, of the town of Lindsay in the riding of the 'Minister of Militia was authorized to purchase blasting'powder for the canal and that his appointment was largely if not entirely due to the bon. Minister of Militia.
Mr. SAM. HUGHES:	I rise to correct
the hon. member on that point. The gentleman to whom he has made reference, Mr. Cinnamon, was never, directly or indirectly, agent for blasting powder on the Trent canal and the Minister of Militia knew absolutely nothing, directly or indirectly, concerning him.

1.	That I am informed and verily believe that my name is mentioned in the investigation that took place before G. Howard Ferguson, K.C., In connection with the affairs of the Trent canal in which it is stated that my name figures a number of times on the pay sheet as a labourer.
2.	That I am informed and verily believe that the following is a synopsis of the report of the said G. Howard Ferguson relating to me:
A. Carr is undoubtedly an assumed name for somt one who drew pay regularly as a labourer during 1906, 1907, 1908 and 1909. After exhaustive inquiry I was unable to find any one of that name who had ever been in Peterborough. The superintendent himself admitted that he could not see where the Government ever got value for some three hundred dollars paid to A. Carr in this way. It is the most glaring piece of fraud practised upon the Government.'
3.	That I never at any time worked as a labourer for the Department of Railways and Canals in connection with the Trent canal nor was I aware until after the investigation herein that my accounts against the Department of Railways and Canals were wrongfully entered in the books of the department for labour

instead of for just claims which I had from time to time against the department.
4.	That during the years 1906, 1907, 1908 and 1909 I was engaged from time to time by Mr. J.	H. McClellan the superintendent of the Trent canal at Peterborough and by his accountant E. S. Clarey as a stenographer and did certain typewriting for them from time to time.
5.	That the charges for my services as a stenographer against the Department of Railways and Canals were made by me in the ordinary course of business as a stenographer and at the regular rates and my accounts were paid from time to time for such services in the ordinary course of business.
6.	That I never at any time charged for such services any excessive amount nor did I ever make any charge against the department except such as I would make against any other customer who might call at my office to have such services performed.
7. This system seemed to have been in general use. Hotelkeepers, boardinghouse keepers, photographers, grocers and others were all treated in the same way. Their bills, I am informed, are actually lying in the office at Peterborough at this moment, but, instead of their bills being sent forward to Ottawa, as would have been proper, their names were put on the pay-list, and they drew that much pay as labourers or

He never called a single witness implicated by McClellan to contradict that statement. The inference I draw from the report is that he did not believe McClellan and that this is what he intended to convey But he should have done it in sterner and more explicit language.
