Mr. SAM. HUGHES: He thought it was a man.

I suppose he did, and consequently they could not find out who it was. I do not think any fault will be found with the commissioner for stating at the time that he did not know who ' A. Carr ' was, who was entered on the pay-list as a labourer, although ultimately it turned out that A. Carr was a typewriter in the office of a firm in Peterborough in which Clarry was interested. There is no reason why, ii typewriting was done for Mr. McClellan or Mr. Clarry or anybody else in connection with the Trent canal, that it should not have been charged for as typewriting and paid for as typewriting.
I agree with that.

But when this account was paid for by putting A. Carr down on the pay-list as a- labourer at a dollar and a half a day, it deceived the department, it deceived the minister, and it deceived everybody else. To pay for typewriting by putting down the name of the typewriter as a day labourer doing work on a dam, seems to me to be altogether wrong. When these facts appeared it would seem to the commissioner or to anybody else that the paying of an account for typewriting in that way must be to cover up

some wrong-doing, because one would naturally suppose that if the account were honest it would be paid for in the usual way. Take the case of a manager of a bank, signing as being paid for so many days' labour. I do not think that is right, and I do not believe any man in the House will think it is right.

Did any bank manager
sign the pay-roll?

Signed the pay-roll. As my
hon. friend knows, the pay-roll is made up every month, it being the regular printed pay-list, and on that list was the name of the bank manager as a labourer for so many days at $1.50 a day.
Mr. GRAHAM I suppose he is not down as a ibank manager?

No, he is down as a labourer, and he receipted the account and got the money. Any bank manager who would do that, I do not care who he is, in my opinion, when he signed the pay-roll, knew that he was doing something that was not right, and as a bank manager he would not allow such a thing to go in his bank.

Have you a pay-roll
there that a bank manager did sign?

I have not got one here, but I will show the hon. gentleman a pay-roll later. I am informed by the officers of the department that that was what was done and that very month these names appeared on the pay-roll. I will ask Mr. Bell as to that. I can understand how some of these others might do it and not know it was wrong, because they are not used to business methods. For instance, Mr. Hewitt might do it without thinking there was anything wrong about it, because he has no business training in such matters. The accountant goes around and says to these men:	Here is a pay-list, sign these
accounts.
Nine-tenths of them would do that.

I take it for granted that so far as the items standing in Mr. Hewitt's name are concerned, the date ' 1910 ' is a clerical error; it should have been 1913. But the only point I wish to make is that amongst those listed as ' labourers,' there are some men who should not have signed as receiving money as labourers; in that they were wrong and deserved censure. Others were not to blame, being ignorant of the way accounts were paid.
Perhaps they did not know what they were signing-were merely shown the space in which to sign.
Would the manager of the Bank of Ottawa, or any other bank, sign for a payment of that kind and not know what he was doing ?
If I saw the form to be signed, I could judge better.

The hon. member for South Wellington claims that the Order in Council was first passed to investigate the matter of explosives. No doubt charges were made of irregularities and the Minister of Railways and Canals ordered the investigation. But when the commissioner went to Peterborough no doubt he heard rumours of other irregularities. It is a good thing the matter was investigated in order that it might be put right. Surely no hon. member will say that it would be right to have this continued. It is the best thing that ever happened, not only for the Trent canal but for Canada generally, that matters of this kind should be found out and put in proper position. I do not say that the men who supplied these goods did it with any wrong intent. But I do blame, and blame very seriously, those men who knew better yet who signed a pay-roll as labourers. Those men did wrong and have earned censure.
So far as concerns supplies for entertaining people visiting the canal-ministers, exministers, or members of Parliament-my opinion is that it would be a great thing for Canada if every member of Parliament could visit all the works under construction in every part of the Dominion, so that we might know better what we are talking about when these matters are brought up in the House. And if the minister or the superintendent invites people there in order that those people may understand the work better and be able to discuss it more intelligently, I see no reason why the accounts should not be paid. But I object to these accounts appearing as payments to labourers instead of appearing for what they really are.
I agree with the hon. minister's statement in a general way. But what does he say of the finding of the commissioner in this respect? Is it not entirely wrong?

The commissioner went into the accounts. And, remember, you may do this extravagantly. But if I were minister of that department or acting at the time, and accounts were sent in for the reception

of visitors of this kind, I would not hesitate to pay them, and let the public know what I had done. If I were in that position and accounts came in in which the manager of a bank and others were shown as being paid as labourers, I would not pay the accounts at all, because I would assume that there was something dishonest about them. I certainly regret that the names of many prominent citizens of Peterborough-
Mr. SAM. HUGHES: And Victoria.

-and Victoria were brought out in this connection. But I do not see how it would be possible for the commissioner to make a report setting forth irregularities, such as putting on the paylist as labourers the names of those who had supplied goods, instead of paying them in a legitimate way, without mentioning names. I do not-see how, without mentioning names, he could justify his conclusion. The hon. gentleman may say: Why not call these men and see what they had to say about it? But there is no dispute about the accounts. So, I cannot see what object there would be in calling many of these parties simply to show that goods had been supplied.
Mr. tsUBNHAM: What about Clark's account in the Examiner office?
Mr. EhlD: I do not know that particular account, it was an account for printing or something of that kind. But even if some of these men had been called they would simply have said: There is an account for goods supplied and ordered by some official of the Trent Valley canal, Mr. McClellan or some other; the account is right, and I was justly entitled to be paid for the goods. Well, no one disputes that. 1 cannot see how the commissioner could send in a report setting forth the facts without giving the names of the parties1. I am sorry that the names of many persons in Peterborough and Victoria were brought into the report, but I cannot see how the commissioner could have done it in any other way if it was in the public interest that a thorough investigation should be made. I believe that this report will have good results not only in respect of the Trent canal but in respect of other canals throughout the Dominion; it will have the result of making the officials in the Department of Eailways and Canals as well as in other departments attend to business more closely and see that nothing of this kind occurs again.

With regard to Stratton's letters and my reading of them, I think it is a well-understood fact that when the mark of privacy or confidence is put upon a letter or document for the purpose of concealing fraud or impropriety, that very facts releases all confidence in the bona fides of the letter. There is no necessity of arguing that matter. As to the labourers, the reason why these persons were put down as labourers was in order that a system of fraud might be carried on successfully. I will give you two instances. Clark was the accountant in the Examiner office. There was an account running in the Examiner office which never should have been there and it was paid by putting Clark down as a labourer. Who will say that that is a proper thing to do?
Itobinson was put down as a labourer.

I am giving you instances in which it was a case of absolute impropriety. Take the unfortunate case of the man Sheridan. Sheridan died and the men on the canal subscribed for a funeral wreath. Their names were put down as labourers; the account was sent to the department and paid and Clarry and these men put the money in their pockets. No doubt this Government is a heaven-sent (government, but how they were on the eve of September 21, 1911, to have all these things flashed upon them is something [DOT]more than I can understand; it gradually unfolded itself. I was on my guard night and day, because I was surrounded by men [DOT]who were as crooked as a ram's horn and I am mighty lucky that I did not get into all sorts of trouble that I never dreamed [DOT]of. When you are in the midst of the enemy, you have to look out, especially *when the enemy is as crooked as a ram's horn.
With regard to Miss Carr, I have already said that I do not know her; nobody seems to know her at all. This circumstance is simply used as a cloak for fraud; everybody thoroughly understands that. It is a very great pity that names of thoroughly honest citizens were improperly used, but we know how that happened. If you want to do a rascally thing, you get behind the name of a man who stands well with the people; that is the artifice of a rascal.
Mr. Denham, president of the Quaker Oats Company of Peterborough, owns large waterpower properties in that district. The superintendent and manager of the Canadian

General Electric Company of Peterborough, Mr. Patterson, also owns large water-powers. Not a day would pass but they would ring roe up time after time saying that the water was improperly handled; that one minute they would have 3,000 horse-power and the next 1,500, and so on. I would say to them: McClellan says so and so. The superintendent would say: That is not right. I said: the first time McClellan goes up to the head waters of the Trent-which are some 120 or 130 miles back, and entirely outside my constituency-we will go up and see what can foe done; you fellows pay your expenses and we will pay outs. We organized an expedition; we had the mayor of Peterborough to represent Peterborough; we had Mr. Denham to represent the Quaker Oats Company, Mr. Patterson to represent the Canadian General Electric and Mr. Sexsmith to represent his constituents. We went up there and we spent the most active two or three days I have spent in years. We were walking day and night, and as for anything in the way of luxury and picnicking, the thing was a perfect farce. We travelled during the night fifteen miles in'a continuous downpour of rain and up to our knees in mud. It is ridiculous to call this luxury; at any rate, it is not what I am accustomed to. I then wrote to Mr. Denham and told him that after Mr. Ferguson's report came out there might be trouble about these things; that certain circumstances might foe misconstrued. I asked him to make a statement and he made a statement in which he said that they paid all their own expenses. The Quaker Oats Company paid Mr. Denham's expenses, the General Electric paid Patterson's and certainly I paid my own. I do not agree with that part of the report which says that the men lived luxuriously; I saw no evidence of luxury. I saw nothing but hard work; some people may call it luxury, but I do not. So far as I was concerned, I refused to stay in Hewitt's house all night, I slept in the automobile. Denham stayed with me for a while, but about two or three o'clock in the morning he said:	I cannot stand
this; I will have to go into the house, which he did.
It will be observed that I did not charge Stratton or any of these men with having a cigar or a bottle of soda along the canal at the Government's expense; as a matter of fact I for one do not think these people are small enough to saddle such things on the Government. I may say by the way that I provided myself by way of estoppel
with a statement from Mr. McClellan that neither personally or politically was I ever engaged in a trip at the expense of the Government. As to this man Clarry, he was the kind of chap of whom we read in the works of Dickens. He was a great little scavenger; there is no question about that. You cannot generalize by quoting single instances, but you can show something to substantiate your assertions. Mr. Clarry got up a history of the Trent Valley canal and thought, I suppose, that he would get a great deal of glory out of the thing. He had it typewritten by Nelson; Nelson was put on as a labourer and was paid for doing this work on the history of the Trent Valley canal for Clarry. Who is going to say that is right? Certainly it is not right; Clarry was not honest. The report shows that the investigation discloses the conditions only on the surface. Anybody who lives in Peterborough or in the Trent district knows perfectly well that if this is what appears after a sort of hen-scratching on the surface, heaven only knows how much there is below.
I asked this man Eastwood:	What do
you mean by all this note shaving of these poor wretches who are employees on the canal; that is thoroughly wrong. He had them listed on a number of sheets of paper. He brought out several of these sheets at the time, and how much do you suppose they would amount to by the summer? I made a calculation myself, and I believe that they amounted between $400 and $500 a year for years. That is what the shoving of 50 cents and 75 cents apiece on all these employees meant. As for Vincent Eastman raising a row because a thing of that kind was discovered in his bank, he had better think again before making another complaint of being caught at that sort of thing, (because in one instance when he was caught he forked over on my demand. He knew that it was wrong, and said so. There is the case of Joseph Yelland, who was a foreman working on the canal. The hon. member for South Wellington, who certainly did himself justice in the dissection of the report, with all his usual skill and intelligence, did not refer to this man. What did Yelland say? He said he was brought in against his will from doing carpenter work on the canal on piers, wharfs, etc., and was rammed into Stratton's committee room for two weeks; he had to stay there in spite of himself, and his time was paid for by the Government. Is that right? The whole thing is

not worth looking into. As a matter of fact, they were a lot of common rascals and they *were caught at it, and that is the whole thing in a nutshell.
I want my friend to except a large proportion of these citizens of Peterborough from the term of rascals.
I do not say all these other people, certainly not. Mr. Gibson is one of my most intimate friends.

This report is another evidence that the principle underlying the appointment of royal commissions is being departed from. The royal commission was intended to be a judicial tribunal, to find out the real facts of a case; but under the present Government we have seen the appointment as commissioners of the very strongest partisans, who are liable tb bring in reports not always warranted by the facts. While the intention in appointing royal commissions was to take investigations out of the political arena and really get at the truth, in at least two cases during this session the reports have been so strongly partisan that you have to go over the evidence very carefully to get at the facts, and you are not much farther ahead after you have read the report than you were before. I do not object to an investigation one iota; what I do object to is that the names of prominent persons, who were within a stone's throw of where thia investigation was held, should be published to the world as having received pay in a manner in which they ought not to have received it, or for work which they never performed. The explanation of the minister is in a way right from his standpoint. But, let us take it home to ourselves. Supposing the name of the hon. member for West Peterborough or myself appeared as implying that we had put in an account for certain services, that we had got our check and receipted it, and then, in a few weeks, it was spread broadcast over the country that we had been fraudulently accepting pay as labourers. I say the commissioner made a great mistake and perpetrated an injustice on a lot of respectable people in Peterborough by not calling them before him and asking them to answer a few questions. From what has come out here to-day, it is evident that members on both sides have unanimously agreed that in nearly every instance these people are altogether innocent of any wrong-doing. Still the public have a suspicion, it has been thrown out in this report that there

is something wrong on their part. So far as the irregularity in the office is concerned, I would not defend it for one moment. These names should never have been put on the pay-list for anything except what they had done or furnished. The proper way to do, no matter what the account is for, is to get a voucher, send in the account and have it passed and paid by cheque to the man, paid for what it was and for nothing else. Any account that cannot be paid in that way is not a legitimate account and should not be paid. There is no doubt about that. But the commissioner did not exercise due diligence to protect the innocent parties in his finding. In reference to Hewitt, I cannot be accused of defending a Liberal, as he is a Conservative, as every one knows. In the county of Hastings and in the surrounding country I have a good many friends and many relatives, and I know this man Hewitt. I would trust Hewett with anything I had.
Hewitt does not live in Hastings.

I said ' and the surrounding country': You will find .some of my relatives in your county-and I am afraid they vote wrong from my point of view. This charge will stick to Hewitt as long as he lives. It should not. No person is called upon to exercise as great care as a man in a semi-judicial position to avoid injuring innocent parties. No name should be used until there has been the fullest investigation. What Hewitt did was absolutely right. That brings me to the point of supplies for visitors. I agree with the acting minister and the member for West Peterborough that that is too picayune for a commissioner to have anything to do with in a report. If the members of this House from the western parts of Canada and from Ontario could be induced to go down over the Intercolonial railway, for instance, mc'e frequently than they do, they wotdd become the strongest advocates of Government ownership of the Intercolonial, because there is no better run road in this country than the Government railway. It would be the same if members of Parliament could be induced to go over the Trent Canal system; they would find that it opens up one of the best tourist districts in America, and one of the most beautiful. Besides it will be useful for freight purposes as well. Any money that is expended in taking members of Parliament or any other prominent men over our public works is money well expended, and I am here to defend it no matter whether the expenditure is made

by-a Conservative or a Liberal. It is all nonsense for a commissioner to take time to bring in findings against anybody for spending a few dollars in taking public men over our public works because tiiat is money well expended.

It is only the way they were paid.
Mr. GRx\HAM:	Ferguson finds the
money was expended in luxurious style. Hewitt spent these large amounts in boarding men working on the canal under contract and I guarantee that if he is like most boardinghouse keepers he did not make much profit.
Mr. SAM. HUGHES:	And he was getting no pay for boarding them.

No, in a sense, and now he has been cut down to $600 a year. Let me say that the minister, notwithstanding this report, should put Hewitt's salary back where it was.
Mr. SAM. HUGHES:	Hewitt boarded
these men and the Government paid the grocers. Now, Hewitt does not board the men but charges them. I understand that he will in future charge any man for any board he gets.

And it will cost the
Government more than before.
Mr. SAM. HUGHES:	But it will free
Hewitt from any charge of graft.

Perhaps I am too tenderhearted but I consider it is most unfair to bring a man, no matter what his views may be, whose only capital is his reputation, and have a report made about him of this kind in which there is absolutely not one word of truth, particularly where the commissioner had before him evidence absolutely contrary to his report. I say that the Government are under some obligation to Hewitt to straighten this thing out. As to the result of the report itself, I earnestly hope that it will be to better methods of account keeping.
It has not been shown except for one or two minor cases that my hon. friend has mentioned, and which I have not had time to look into, that any moneys paid ought not to have been paid; therefore, in that respect there has been no loss to the country. The most that can be said- although I am not here to defend any person-is that the system of book-keeping used in the office was very efficient, and I am glad to hear that that is to be changed.
I would advise the officials engaged on the Trent Valley canal or any other officials not to do this kind of thing-no matter who asks them. When money has to be spent let it be spent in the proper way; send the accounts into the department and have them O.K.'d by the auditor, and then if there is any wrong-doing it will not be the fault of the officials.
As my name has been mentioned I would like to make a little explanation.
The apology is accepted.

Some time in the early part of July of last year, Mr. Denham, the manager of the Quaker Oats Company in Peterborough, told me over the ' phone that he was arranging a party to look over the Trent Valley water system with a view to its power possibilities, and asked me if I would be kind enough to make one of the party. I accepted not with any idea of having a picnic but with the object of gaining some knowledge of the Trent Valley waters. I agree with the hon. member for W est Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) that it was no picnic; in fact, it was the hardest two or three days I ever put in my life. I went on Mr. Denham's invitation, and I understood that the Quaker Oats people were paying their share of the trip. Even if the Government paid for it I think it would have been perfectly justified.
Do not do it again.

I would do it again
under similar conditions.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Miscellaneous-British Columbia better terms commission, $40,000.
What is the work being done by this commission?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This is the Better Terms Commission. The position of the matter at the present time is that British Columbia prepared its case and some discussion between the two Governments took place as to whether the claims set forth in the case did not extend beyond the scope of the commission. After negotiations in regard to that, an arrangement was made that certain claims should not be pressed, and the case is being amended. I believe that the amended case is about

499=

ready and that as soon as the amended ease has been filed the case for Canada will be filed. In the meantime, the chairman has not been appointed. The reason that he has not been appointed is that we are desirous to know, before making the appointment, how long the proceedings will probably occupy and where the meetings will be held. It is difficult to give very definite information about these matters until both cases are filed.

Who represents the
Dominion Government?
Mr. Martin.
An excellent appointment.
Eoughly, what is the contention on the part of British Columbia? What do they claim in the way of better terms?

They claim that the
natural conditions of the province are very different from those in other provinces and call for enormous expenditures on public works in the way of putting in roads, bridges, etc. They build roads there which cost, I think, $20,000 a mile.

No doubt certain miles
would cost that.
They put forward a claim of that character. It was presented, in the first place, at the Interprovincial Conference about eight or ten years ago.
I understood that at that time their claim was for an additional $100,000 a year by way of subsidy. Is that the limit of their claim?

No, they got the $100,000 additional at that time, and it was desired that they should accept that in full. The resolutions which were presented to the conference, and which formed the foundation of the resolutions presented to this House, declared that it should be in full. But when the Imperial Act was framed, founded upon an address to His Majesty which had been passed by this House at the time, that particular provision was not inserted, as it was held it would be an attempt to fetter the future action of Parliament.
About how much do they claim, or has that come to the attention of the Government yet?

I do not think that they have put it in the form of an exact state-
ment of the amount. They simply put -forward certain matters upon which they base a claim for further financial consideration. My recollection is that no exact amount is named.

Is it to be understood
that the Dominion is contesting that claim, or has the Dominion an alternative proposition to make?

No, we have no alternative proposition to make. We shall endeavour to put the case on behalf of the Dominion in an effective way. The case on behalf of the Dominion has not yet been submitted to me, and it has not yet been prepared, but the preparation of it has been entrusted to Mr. Martin, K.C., of Montreal, acting in conjunction with the Minister of Justice and the Deputy Minister of Justice.
What is the composition of the commission? I understand the chairman has not been appointed. How are the other members of the commission appointed?

The Government of British Columbia appoint one, the Government of Canada appoint another, and the Secretary of State for the Colonies appoints the third. Provided that the two commissioners could have agreed, they would have appointed the third, but they were not able to come to an agreement, g,nd therefore we had to call upon the Secretary of State for the Colonies to appoint the third commissioner, who will be the chairman.
Pensions

To provide for the payment of a pension to Mrs. Mary E. Fuller, on account of services of Simon J. Dawson, negotiating with the Indian tribes in the lake of the Woods district, 1869-1873, $600.
What is the explanation of that?

Mr. Dawson, as reported to me by officers of the Department of the Interior, had, for a certain number of years-I think about four years-performed very important services on behalf of the Government in connection with the incidents alluded to in the item. At that time he did not receive any compensation whatever from the Government for his services, but they are regarded by the officers of the Interior Department as being very valuable. This lady is his only remaining relative. The matter has no doubt been before my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver).

No, I do not recollect
that it has.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Then I think my hon.
friend is the only person to whnss attention it has not been called because it has been brought forward by a great many hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House and in the Senate as well; in fact, it has been pressed very strongly on my attention ever since we came into office. There was no opportunity to look into it very carefully until last year and then I asked some of the members of the Privy Council to consult with the officers of the Department of the Interior and to come to a conclusion as to the merits of the case. My recollection is that Mr. Perley made a very careful investigation and reported that he thought the circumstances were such that a small pension might properly be granted to Mrs. Fuller.
This is supposed to be an annual payment?
Yes.

What is the relationship
between Mrs. Fuller and the late Mr. Dawson?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
She is the only relative
who survives him and she is in very needy circumstances.
Perhaps this case might encourage my right hon. friend to consider favourably the case I mentioned this afternoon.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is some force in
what my hon. friend says.

I have no doubt as to
the value of the services rendered by Mr. Dawson, although I am not personally familiar with them. I know that he did give valuable service to the country in the early days of the acquirement of the Northwest, and later on. The only question about this vote is as to the relationship between Mrs. Fuller and the late Mr. Dawson, which does not appear to be very close.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My recollection is,
although I am not sure, that this lady was dependent on Mr. Dawson during his lifetime. It is quite clear that Mr. Dawson never did receive any consideration for the services he rendered.

I am quite sure he
rendered services that were never put on the books, but if the Government is entering upon a general policy of pensions, I would like to mention to my right hon. friend the 3151
case of the widow of the late William Ogilvie, once Governor of the Yukon.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That has been brought to my attention and I shall endeavour to have it considered by the sub-committee of the Privy Council.
Militia-Annual drill, $2,000,000.
There is an increase in this item?

The force to be drilled this year will be greater than last year, by several thousand men. We have also increased the pay for horses twenty-five cents a day, and the rations for the men will cost five cents per day more.

How many men will
drill this year?
About 63,000.
I see that the members of Parliament are invited to the camps.

I have done myself the honour to invite the members of Parliament. I have again and again seen in the past that when members of Parliament have come to the camps no recognition is extended to them, and it has always seemed to me that that is not right. The officers were delighted last year to entertain such members of Parliament as honoured them with a visit.
Will the minister guarantee there will be no one to see how much we eat, as was the case on the Trent canal?
Will we have to bring our baskets?
No, the culinary department will be properly equipped.

Yesterday, when the Bill to give relief to the depositors of the Farmers Bank was under consideration, the Minister of Finance said that the amounts to be paid to the depositors, would not be liable to be seized under execution for debt. Is there any regulation in the Militia Department to the effect that the $100 Fenian Raid bounty cannot be seized under the Collection of Debt Act or under execution for debt. Again, suppose the veteran who if living would be entitled to a bounty, died unmarried, and had been living with some near relative, who would be entitled to the bounty?

All that is arranged by the Minister of Finance. We issue the certificate and the Department of Finance issues the cheque. I had a consultation

with the Minister of Finance on the matter, and the Minister of Finance in order to meet the case mentioned by my hon. friend 'will take the precaution to see that the *cheque shall not be subject to garnishee. I understand the law says that the money shall be paid to the legal representatives of the deceased.

I have in mind the case of an old man who died a short time ago, who before he died had his property taken away by his creditors and he went to live with his daughter-in-law.
Letters of administration will likely be taken out, and the administrator will be required to pay to the creditors, unless there is some regulation to prevent it. In such a case as I have spoken of, the creditors should not be allowed to have any portion of the money.

The daughter should
have it. As I understand it, the cheque goes direct to the legal representative and cannot be sidetracked. Whether the Finance Minister will agree to divert it contrary to the statute I cannot say. But there will be few of such cases.

The departments, as
a rule, do not recognize an assignment under local statutes?

I understand they do
not.

Several cases have come under my notice which the minister will probably be asked to pass upon. In case of the death of the volunteer, the money must bo paid to the widow or legal representative, but to establish the position of the legal representative resort rnnsr be had to the courts which may cost a large proportion of the $100.

Formerly, in case of the death of the soldier, letters of administration had to be taken out. But under the new law which has been passed, it is provided that the money shall be paid to the widow or legal representative.

But the man may die
intestate leaving no will, and to pay to the ' legal representative ' means going to the court.
But that would be necessary in any case.

This $100 may be the
only thing in the world belonging to these

people, and it would be a pity to have it eaten up in costs.
I understand the Minister of Finance has authority to settle that matter by Order in. Council.
Does the Order in Council control as against the statute ?
He can make it payable to the widow, or, if there is no widow, to the next legal representative.
That is exactly the trouble-there you get back to the creditors. Why not make it payable to a son or daughter living with him ?
I understand such cases have to be submitted to the Department of Justice, and that is beyond my sphere. But there has been little trouble in these cases so far.
The minister will endeavour, as far as possible, to deal with this $100 as a bounty, and not as due to the deceased ?
That is the rule of the department.
In the case of an application. being sent in which the person is mistaken in his qualifications, is the applicant notified?
Every time. Immediately. We take it for granted that every application is absolutely honest. We show the applicant where he has fallen down and ask him to substantiate his case.

I was writing to some persons as to their applications and I find that in some cases the affidavits are not authenticated as having been sworn before a commissioner. I was going to write to Mr. Panet, who is always very courteous-
Very kind. If the hon. gentleman will drop him a line, any explanation will be given.
Only one word more. I hope the department will as speedily as possible pay these claims. It would take a great deal of trouble from everybody who has to do with the county.
We are paying now at the rate of about two hundred and fifty a day.
' Does the department insist upon the certificate of death from the official issuer of death certificates?
We follow the legal form, whatever it is.

I understand that the department has been insisting upon a certificate of death. Of course, the official certificate is the best evidence of death. But other evidence ought to be accepted in its absence. Suppose a widow making application. She swears that she is the widow of a certain deceased, who died on such a day. This is certified by the comrade of deceased, who says that he knew A- B- in his lifetime, and that said A- B- wa3 enrolled in the regiment. Why should not those two declarations be accepted instead of an official certificate?
I do not see why not.

A few evenings ago a discussion took place with reference to veterans' claims. I was called out of the House at that time. I have a matter I desire to call to the attention of the minister, the case of those who took part in repelling the raid that took place in Manitoba in 1871. Oldtimers in Manitoba will remember that we had a Fenian Raid from across the border in that year. Colonel Irwin was then in command of the permanent force in Winnipeg. He took the permanent force from Winnipeg to the boundary line accompanied by one hundred volunteers from the city of Winnipeg to replace the invaders, Before leaving he called on Captain George Newcombe, of Poplar Point, and instructed him to bring a company from that place, known as the Poplar Point Rifles, to hold the fort in 'his absence-old Fort Garry at Winnipeg. Mr. Newcombe, who is now in the employ of the Department of the Interior, came into Winnipeg with one hundred settlers armed, took possession of the Fort and held it. Mr. E. G. G. Hay, one of the old-timers of Manitoba,	one of Manitoba's oldest and
most	respected citizens, brought up
about fifty men from St. Andrews which is in my own county and joined Captain Newcombe's force. This combined force held the Fort for fifteen to eighteen days while Colonel Irwin was at the boundary. These men were under arms and were paid by Colonel Peebles who was the paymaster under Governor Archibald at that time. I claim that every one of these men is entitled to any grant to be paid to Fenian Raid veterans. I am satisfied that if it had not been for the fact that Colonel Irwin went to the front with his force of one hundred and fifty men-one hundred volunteers and the rest regulars-and from the calling in of the volunteers of Manitoba to hold Fort Garry, the affair would have been much more serious than it turned out to be. My ibon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) brought up this matter a few nights ago and I wish to supplement what he so well said on that occasion. These men ought to be taken care of. A good many of them are living at the present time. I have been petitioned time after time, and I have petitioned the department on this subject, but I must say I have received no encouragement that the case of these men should be considered.
I think that the claims of these men ought to be considered. There is no doubt, as in the case of a man like Mr. Hay, who is a very old man, that the $100 is not a very great consideration to many of these persons, but it seems to me that they ought to receive recognition just the same as others who have taken part in the defence of the country.
Mr, HUGHES: The veterans of the Red river rebellion of 1870 were granted their scrip; those who took part in the Northwest rebellion of 1885 got their scrip also, and those who went to South Africa got their scrip. In consequence the old veterans, of 1866, many of whom turned out and gave weeks of actual service, thought themselves slighted; hence the agitation of the veterans of 1866 and 1867. Owing perhaps, to the fact mentioned by my hon. friend, that the people of Manitoba were in such good circumstances that they did not have any desire to apply for the bounty, at the time this Bill was put through we had no applications from the people of the Northwest. The facts brought up by the hon. member for Edmonton were laid before the Assistant Adjutant General; he looked into the matter, but it was too late to do anything this year.

Some of the Fenian
Raid veterans have been inquiring of me as to whether or not they will be entitled to receive their medals after they have qualified for the bounty. Quite a number of persons did not apply for the medals when they were being granted, and they are now looking for them. I should like to have some indication from the minister as to what his policy is in regard to conferring medals upon veterans who are receiving the bounty.

My predecessor had the necessary legislation passed whereby these

people automatically become entitled to medals. Proof that a man is entitled to the $100 is proof that he is entitled to a medal.
All they have to do is apply?
I do not know that they even have to do that.
Are the medals of gold or of silver?
Silver.
Are they available now?

No, the medals have to be obtained-I think some of them are in now-and	then the name has to be
engraved on the rim, that takes a little time.

Does the minister know
whether or not the volunteers who served in the raids referred to by the hon. member for Selkirk have been considered eligible for medals and if any applications have been made?

The matter has never
been considered by me. I do not know what my predecessor did in the matter; I shall look it up and let my hon. friend know if he so desires.

I may say that when the Bill was first brought down mentioning the dates 1866, 1870 and 1871, it never occurred to me for one moment that the men who took active part in the Manitoba raid were not included.

We in Manitoba all understood that they were eligible.

Does the department
grant anything to the Boy Scout movement?

A number of boys were taken from the town of Glace Bay last year to go into camp at Kentville; is that under the Department of Militia?

cadet system.
That will go on this year also?
Yes.

What is the general scope of the assistance the department gives in the way of taking these school boys away during the holiday'5 Mr. HUGHES: We ration and transport them, but we do not pay them. The theory is that the boys would outgrow uniforms, so we contribute $1 a year towards their clothing.

I wish to refer for a moment to an order which has recently been issued forbidding the 65th regiment in Montreal to accompany the host on Corpus Christi day. I hold no brief for the Church, but this matter has created quite a turmoil in Montreal, and I should like to know from the hon. gentleman exactly the nature of the orders which have been issued. I may say, en passant, that for thirty years we have had in Montreal the 65th Regiment, composed almost exclusively of Catholics, and every year this regiment takes its place in the ranks of the procession on Corpus Christi day. The question, I suppose, is whether or not the regiment should bear arms. Would my hon. friend explain the matter, and set at rest the many rumours which are afloat? In reading not long ago a history of old Quebec immediately after the British conquest, I observed that on Corpus Christi day the British regiments garrisoned at Quebec formed a guard of honour when the host was passing through the streets of the old capital. Of course, that is not within my personal knowledge; as I have said, I read it in a history of the old days of Quebec immediately after British domination commenced. To my knowledge, for the last thirty years the 65th Battalion in Montreal, to which some members of my family once belonged, has always formed a guard of honour on that day. Last year several battalions in Montreal took part in a race around the mountain, organized by the Montreal Star. To that I have no objection, but the criticism against the decision of the minister, as

given by the newspapers, is to this effect: that if the regiments of Montreal are allowed to take part in a race organized by an enterprising newspaper, there is no reason why the regiment composed exclusively of Catholics should be debarred from taking part in the procession on Corpus Christi. Besides, my hon. friend himself has set the example; last year he attended the very fine demonstration held at St. Irenee. Our friend and colleague the hon. member for Charlevoix and Montmorency (Sir Eodolphe Forget) is the honorary colonel of the 65th Battalion, and I am bound to say that he has done a great deal for that regiment.
Last year there was a demonstration at St. Irenee. The whole regiment was invited; the Minister of Militia was present, and a religious service was held. Somebody, I do not know whether the information is reliable or not, stated that at the moment of the blessing, when my hon. friend knelt down with the officers and soldiers, he made the sign of the cross, but with the left hand. Of course this is only hearsay. However, he was present himself and he can testify that there was nothing pernicious and nothing mysterious against the mother country in any of those demonstrations. In fact they ought to be encouraged. The man who serves his God will naturally serve his country. I hope that the explanation the minister will give will set at rest the excitement which exists among those who belong to the regiment. At present no such explanation has been given, and I could read from the press which is friendly to the Government very bitter criticism concerning the orders given by my hon. friend. I do not understand why the order has been issued. It does not do any harm to see the regiment in a procession, especially if the regiment is composed exclusively of Catholics; nor do I object, at a church parade, to see the Protestant soldiers go to their respective churches as the Catholics go to theirs. My hon. friend on Sunday last was himself present at a church parade in Montreal and I suppose that the 65tli was one of the regiments which took part in it. I do not see why, if you permit regiments to go to their respective churches carrying their arms, you should object to seeing Catholic regiments forming a guard of honour at a Catholic demonstration or a Protestant regiment at a Protestant demonstration, the regiment being present and adding to the dignity of the ceremony.

I am not aware from
what source the hon. gentleman gets the
inspiration that I have issued any order. The regulation is as old as the militia * system and I have made no change of any kind. Perhaps I can best explain it by reading an interview which appears in today's Montreal Gazette, as follov'?:
Col. the Hon. Sam Hughes, Minister of Militia and Defence, interviewed to-day concerning the regulation about carrying of arms by soldiers in religious processions and the agitation emanating from Montreal concerning it, said:
'No order or regulation, directed against any corps, any creed, or any race, concerning the carrying of arms in church parades, or religious processions, has been issued by me.'
'The regulation is as old as the hills, and the practice still older, that when troops attend divine service they never carry arms. There are only two exceptions throughout the Empire to this regulation, one is active service, in presence of an enemy and the other is in India and kindred places. The arms, in both cases, are carried so that in case of sudden emergency the troops would be ready for active service.'
The minister could scarcely comprehend the statement that he had any objection to troops taking part in any divine service. "Why,' said he, ' at St. I rf-nfe, in Quebec, last year, I was more than pleased to join the 65th Regiment of Montreal in their divine service. Indeed, if I had time nothing would give me greater pleasure than going to Montreal again this coming Sunday and marching with the boys *f the 65th to their divine service.'
The rule is, and it is certainly not a new one, that side arms only are worn.
'On two occasions,' continued Col. Hughes, 'within recent months, the Department of Militia and Defence has had to refuse permission for two corps, almost entirely Protestant, to have their rifles for Sunday operations. For the life of me, I cannot see why any one would want to carry a rifle to divine service. I have yet to find an officer, of any creed, who endorses the carrying of rifles, or who takes exceptions to this well established rule.'
In church parades they carry only side arms?

Yes, only. There is no objection in the world to the 65th or any other regiment doing that. The 65th has a warm spot in the corner of my heart. I attended divine service with them last year and whether or not they suffered from my presence, I certainly was not a bit the worse of it. It was a very nice service and a very nice sermon upon 'duty.'

Was it before you left
for Europe?

Yes, it was while I was on the tour in a special train to the Maritime provinces. I might point out that there is nothing in the world under the regulations to prevent the 65th turning out for divine service to-morrow the same as they

did last Sunday, and if I were in Montreal nothing would afford me greater pleasure than to walk out with the officers and boys of the regiment, and I would have not the slightest hesitation in taking part in the .service. But the regulation is there and I see no reason why it should be changed. Personally I think it would be quite out of place to have the rifles in church.

This seems satisfactory, but what about the custom? I think if the custom was maintained and if published in the press, all this misunderstanding will be cleared.
Mr. OLIVER; What has been the custom in the past in regard to the carrying of arms at church services? When the 65th paraded last Corpus Christi day did they carry arms?
I do not know.

Yes, they have always carried arms.
Militia and Defence-Clothing, $800,000. ,
Who has the contract for the clothing?

The contractors are in
various places. They are the same old contractors. When my predecessor took office he was imbued with the idea of changing the contractors and he did so with great loss to the country, and finally had to go back to the old contractors. When we took office we became virtuous and tried to change the contractors, but we met with loss and delay and all sorts of trouble on the part of contractors and failure on the part of men who, in the course of years would, probably have become as expert as the employees of the old contractors. The old men have beep doing this kind of work for years and can do it much more satisfactorily and therefore we are still giving them the contracts.
Militia and Defence-Contingencies, $44,000.
What does that cover?

This is for expenses not provided for in other votes, such as telegraphing and telephoning, advertising, allowances to officiating clergymen at the permanent force stations, legal expenses, guards of honour, etc. This vote is a little less than last year.

I suppose that covers
the duty on the uniforms?
Yes, we have to pay duty on everything that is imported just the same as any other person.

It is just taking money
out^of one pocket of the Government and putting it into another.
Yes. I tried to persuade the Minister of Customs to allow this cloth to come in free but he would .not come around to my view.

I saw an item in the
paper the other day that temperance beer had been smuggled into Petawawa camp. I understand that my hon. friend is going to prevent temperance beer from entering the camp in future.
I was not aware that we were going to stop temperance beer from coming in. The intention is to stop nontemperance beer.

I understand that the
beer was put out because it was temperance beer.

About this clothing. I see the minister intends to buy 10,000 pairs boots, 50,000 shirts, 30,000 pairs of trousers and 20,000 pairs of pants. I do not understand the difference between trousers and pants, myself. How does my hon. friend buy these articles? Does a tailor who is not supporting the present Administration get a chance to make any of these articles?
M. HUGHES: I was just telling the exMinister of Railways that unfortunately or otherwise, most of the work is done by the old contractors with the late Government. A new boot man, however, underbid the others by 15 or 20 cents and has been given the contract.
Mr. WM. CHISHOLM: In the Kingston Penitentiary report I think the suggestion was made that a lot of these boots, shoes, harness, clothing, etc., for the militia could be made by the prisoners, to the advantage of the prisoners and the country as well, because the prisoners could do it more cheaply. Does the minister intend to act on the suggestion of the commission?

The matter has not been brought to my attention before, but I will be glad to confer with the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice and my other colleagues about it. The ordinary industries of the country object very strongly to the penitentiaries coming into active competition with industrial concerns, and I can quite understand that. I can see very

good reasons for employing prisoners in making roads and things of that kind, but undoubtedly there would be great opposition from the workingmen of the country if the penitentiaries entered , into competition with industrial concerns manufacturing clothing, boots and things of that kind.
iMr. GRAHAM: I appreciate the difficulty, but if the manufactures of these penitentiaries were all made for Government consumption, they would not be coming in competition with outside trade. The Government would be simply manufacturing for its own consumption. It is a difficult thing to deal with, and many ways have been tried of meeting the difficulty. <One thing is sure: the prisoners have to be provided with work of some kind, and, in my opinion, breaking stone is not proper work for prisoners except for a very peculiar class.

In regard to this clothing, I am credibly informed that in the case of the scarlet uniforms in a particular locality I have in mind, the dye is so poor that one shower of rain is sufficient to make it run and destroy the whole appearance of the uniform, and consequently its usefulness. I had always understood that the scarlet uniform was of the very best quality, both as to material and colour, and it is rather a shock to my ideas to find [DOT] such an accusation existing. If the Grit contractors have control of that output at the present time, I would respectfully suggest that the minister make a change.

Hitherto the tunics and trousers have been supplied by three or four contractors, who are permitted to buy their own scarlet cloth. The result has been that the uniforms varied as to texture, colour and .strength of dye. To meet the difficulty we are now buying our own cloth and selling it to these contractors.
I do not wish to pose as an authority on military matters, but I would like to know if the different kinds of uniforms in use in the militia are for ornament or for use.	.

I think that my hon. friend shows that he has a good military head, and would make a second Clive or Nicholson. Of course, all the volunteers like to have as nice a uniform as possible on show days in the towns and cities, and that is a very proper spirit. About a year ago we decided to issue a khaki uniform as well. The ornamental dress is now
reserved for review days. Whereas formerly the ornamental uniform would last only about two years, by being reserved in this way it will last four or five. We are making a two years' issue of uniforms; in other words, we are making money for the Government by supplying uniforms for two years because we are making the fine uniforms last twice as long as they formerly did. Let any one take a nice uniform to camp and lie around for a week or two and it is gone. We preserve these fine uniforms for show purposes in cities and towns, or for home entertainment, or for review day and provide the khaki uniform for camp.

Will the honorary
colonels be subject to the same limits as the other officers?
Yes, and if the 41st of Broekville, or the 42nd of Renfrew, recommends my hon. friend as an honorary colonel we will put him on the list.
Shall I have to buy the uniform myself?
Here is something that is not generally realized by the public; the cost of the gold lace -and all that sort of thing has to be borne by the officers themselves, which I think is entirely wrong.

Are these honorary
colonels for ornament or for use?
My predecessor appointed about 144 and I have appointed less than half of that number. I am sorry to say that my hon. friend is not on the list.

There are still a few
who have not been appointed.
Yes, some remain; but while the lamp holds out to burn
I am not anxious for it.
Our files contain a great many letters from gentlemen who say: Could you not appoint so and so an honorary colonel?

I hope that they have
not mentioned me.

I venture to say that my hon. friend would be at the tailor's next day after he was appointed to get a nice uniform made.
Mr. GRAHAM. He would have to go the banker's first.

In England all these officers are recommended because of some special qualification they possess, such as the man at the head of a railway company, to be of use to the service. Heads of railways, for instance, take a personal interest in the transport of troops to camp. Why should not a railway man who is skilled in his work be a colonel as well as some dub who is entrusted with some other part of the service ?

All officers, not only honorary colonels, but others, have to buy their own uniforms and pay duty on them. In the case of the men their uniforms are bought by the Government, and when the Customs duties are paid it is a matter of taking money out of one pocket and putting it into another, as the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has said. It seems like imposing an unnecessary expense on officers to require that they should pay duty on their uniforms. I would like to ask the minister if he has ever tried to exert any influence on the Minister of Customs to get him to strike out the duty on officers' uniforms.

We tried the first two years, but my hon. friend the Minister of Customs was absolutely stony-hearted, and this year we have placed a sum in the Estimates for that purpose. An item was first voted to pay the duty on all our material, and we tried to bring uniforms in under this item last year, but we could not do so because the vote was for the specific purpose of paying the duty on the material used by the department. This year we are putting an item' in the Estimates to meet the objection of my hon. friend, and I may say that we are doing so in consequence of the public urgings of himself and others. We propose to pay the duty on certain things that have to be imported and that cannot be made in Canada.

Why should not these men pay duty on the articles they wear just as well as the farmers, labourers, miners and people generally ? If they have the honour and glory of wearing a goodlooking suit, why should they object to paying duty more than any other man ?

I know there is a feeling abroad that the officer is there for show, but any one who has been through the service knows how frequently he has to go down in his pocket to pay expenses. For instance, he has to go to the expense of his uniform.
Pay him right.
He has to pay for it, but he wears it in the service of the country, and the least the Government should do is to let him have it free of duty.

There is something in
what the minister says, particularly in regard to the expense. I have had some experience, once removed, of the expense of an officer in a regiment. While my son was living at home, I know that what he got for his service in the regiment did not pay one-twenty-fifth of what it cost me for his company. It costs officers a good deal of money that the public do not know *anything about.
, Mr. LEMIEUX: Would that apply to the .minister's Windsor uniforms?
i Mr. HUGHES: I must say that it made [DOT]me squirm a little when I had to pay the duty on mine.
, Mr. OLIVER: I had the honour to put .before the House, when the Militia Estimates were up last year, a certain view in regard to this matter of officers' uniforms. In my humble judgment, as one *who has every regard for the idea of a volunteer militia and desires to see it a success, as one who has never been in the militia force and does not ever intend to be, not even as an honorary colonel, looking v at the matter solely as an outsider, there should be a complete revision of the relationship between the volunteer force and the department generally .before we will get *a satisfactory service. This idea that [DOT]somebody has to keep up the company is not in accordance with Canadian conditions 'or the democratic ideals that prevail in this country. If the service is worth anything, it is worth its cost to the country. The men who are in it, whether they are privates or officers, are doing their duty in giving their time, energy and talent, and if the country is not able or willing to put up the cost which is necessary to keep the service going, provide uniforms and equipment and other facilities for doing its work, then -the country is not right. We have not that spirit that we ought to have, and I would like to have the matter brought to a show-down and tried out with the people as to whether or not they are willing to pay for the services that they get at the hands of our volunteer organizations.
If .they are not willing to pay then there is nothing more to be said; let them do without the service. If the matter were

put on this basis I believe the people are willing to pay, and I believe we would get a more enthusiastic and consequently a more efficient service than we have now. The existing conditions of the volunteer service are not in accordance with Canadian conditions or with the democratic ideals that prevail in this country, and the sooner they are brought into proper perspective the better for everybody.

The ideas expressed by
the hon. member are certainly along the right lines, and I should imagine that to carry them out to their ultimate end would mean the old system of compulsory training that they used to have in Nova Scotia. We have a purely voluntary system, and that means approaching the men and getting them to go out. I venture to say that there is hardly an officer of the militia service of the Dominion who is not to-day looking after the boys and endeavouring to get them to go to camp. The officer is not going to be mean about it and he probably in many instances takes them to his home and gives them a little supper, and that is what I meant by the expense coming in. In the voluntary system the officers have to approach the men; it cannot be avoided. Taking the compulsory system as an alternative, I am absolutely in favour of the voluntary system. By a little energy and direction on the part of those specially interested, the voluntary system can Ibe made just as effective as any other system. In South Africa they have a voluntary system but there is this tag on it, that any man who has not done his annual training for a certain number of days has to contribute to the state. In Switzerland, they have compulsory service, and the man who for any reason does not do service has to pay a sum into the State treasury. I am delighted to see the stand that my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) takes. Owing to the remarks the hon. gentleman made last year, we are making preparations to carry out a plan, and we are getting ready to do it as soon as possible, to give each officer a drill uniform whenever he qualifies.

Do I understand the
Minister of Militia to accept the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) to have a show-down, and to say he will run the next election on this issue?

Oh, no; my hon. friend
(Mr. Oliver) is merely making a suggestion.
The next election is too far away.
I do not want the Minister of Militia to put me in the position of advocating compulsory service.
No, no.

I do not understand that
will be the consequence of the suggestion I made. I would like to have either a free service or no service at all.

We have a free service
now.
Militia and Defence

Was there not some scandal about the Quebec arsenal? I think I saw it in the newspapers.

There was no scandal. I want to be fair to the late superintendent of the arsenal, and to say that whatever faults were there, were not of his creation. He is a very good officer, but the machinery got out of tune. However, it is all in good shape now.
I do not know anything about it, except what was stated in the newspapers.

Yes. I might mention

What does the Minister of Militia know about the proposed armoury at Edmonton? The Minister of Public Works has given us some information, but

perhaps the Minister of Militia will give us more.

As the hon. member
knows, Edmonton met us splendidly; gave us an entire square, which, I am told, is worth from $150,000 to $250,000-for a drill hall site. I have urged the Minister of Public Works as speedily as possibly to provide drill halls for Edmonton, Calgary and Regina. These will be practically of the same kind and will be as good drill halls as are to be found in the Dominion. These three cities are entitled to that. The Minister of Public
Works informed us the contract had been let last fall. Nothing could be done in the winter, but what I want to know is whether it is being proceeded with this spring?

The people of New Glasgow promised a site some time ago. They picked out a place but had to get legislation from the provincial Legislature to secure a title or something of that kind. Is provision made for
building?	.
