Militia and Defence-Engineer services and works, $916,500.
There are a lot of items in this.
The hon. gentleman will observe we have reduced that item by $288,600

How man rifle ranges
have we?

In that vote we have
$100,000 for rifle ranges. We bought one at Peterborough recently. We are getting a few each year, acquiring them as rapidly as we can.

What is the situation in
regard to the rifle range at Edmonton that has been used for the past two years? Is the ownership of that property in the Dominion Government?
Yes, in the department.
Is that range still in use?

Yes, but it is getting
dangerous. As the hon. member knows better than I do, settlement, thick settlement, is going on at the rear of that range. While the hills are high we do not feel it is any too safe. Every precaution is taken, and we have been trying to get a new range, as the hon. gentleman knows, for I have spoken to him about it and asked him to take it up with others. We could sell the present range, and with one-tenth of the money we could buy a range out in the country. I have picked out two, but the difficulty is one cannot get to them without walking two or three miles. If the hon. gentleman will consult his friends and the military boys there in Edmonton and pick out a range, we will sell the old range and buy that.
What area is required?

We should have 2,500 yards in rear of the target to provide for the range of the new long-range rifle, and fully 1,000 yards in front-practically two and a quarter miles is needed in order to be safe. In fact, sometimes the bullets will fly beyond that. If the country is of a character to enable us to get a big bank behind the target, we can do with ground of less length.
What width is required?
That depends on the number of targets. For a range such as would be required at Edmonton, I should think from a third to a half-mile. You would want several targets for a large city like Edmonton.
The survey there is in mile-square sections, cut into quarters. So it would be practically necessary to buy by quarter-sections. I take it that a quarter-section in width would do?
That is about right.
And five quarter-sections in length?
We could do with four in length by putting up a high stop butt.
As to the character of the country, does it make any difference whether it is level or not for the two miles in length required?
As to the back part, the rougher the better, but for the front we like it level.
Does it make much difference if it is not level?
No, we can get along, if we can get the firing point.
In this item is $100,000 for Connaught rifle range. I suppose that is the one in South March. What is the explanation of this item?

We are asking a vote in the supplementaries to complete it. The old rifle range is estimated to be worth about a million and a quarter of dollars or more. We do not want to sell that until we have got the other. These items should not be charged against, the militia vote, because this is a transference of account. We are building a range with 538 targets, as against 67 on the old range. The old range is entirely inadequate. If members will go down on Saturday afternoon, they will find that every target is occupied with volunteers from Toronto. This is a Dominion range, not one for the locality only. It is for the use of the schools of musketry that are carried on here and other similar purposes.

I understand this
range is to be one of the finest in America.
In the world.
I suppose the cost will be proportionate?
The total cost will be upwards of $600,000. It will be finished this year.
I desire to call attention to the rifle range, between Chatham Lots and Nappan Lots. It was surveyed a year ago; when is it to be completed?
Provision is made for that. A survey is being carried out and the plans are going through the department.
I desire to ask about the range at Stratford, in my county. Negotiations were on for the establishment of a range.
I think there was some hitch, about the purchase of a property.
About the road?
Yes, the road across it. There had to be some county legislation to fix it up. My engineers are looking after that.
There are two companies of mounted infantry-one at Vegreville and one at Lloydminster. Where do they hold their rifle practice?
I could not say.

I am informed by members of the company that they never have any practice at all. It seems to me that if there is any reason for equipping the companies and training them, they should at least have some rifle practice.
The rule is to carry on that practice in annual camp.
That would be at Calgary?
I presume so.
Would the minister consider a rifle range 17 miles from Edmonton to be too far distant from the city?
Is there access by rail?

The minister knows that a few years ago a site along the river was offered to the Militia Department by Major Griesbach. There is a cut bank of 85 feet in height between the river level and the table land above. It was thought at the time that the department was going to make some arrangements in the matter, but nothing has been done. I know that that range is available at the ordinary price of land, $25 or $30 an acre. The late minister made an examination of this property when he visited the West, and he admitted that it was the best site he had seen. If this range were established the three companies would have a place to practice. I may say that the mounted police have not been able to have any practice on account of lack of a rifle range.
I will look into the matter.
Did I understand the minister to say that an amount is provided in the Estimates to build the rifle range to which I referred?
Not specifically; it is in the general vote and the work is going on.

What arrangements
have been made in connection with the school of instruction at Winnipeg?
The plan is to build on the old government ground out there; nothing is settled as yet.
A year ago I had a conversation with the minister about the grants to the bands.
I carried out my promise to the hon. gentleman and increased the grant by fifty per cent.

I am glad to know the
minister has done so, because these bands are universally good and useful.

The explanation given by the minister as to the use made of the Royal Canadian Regiment Band in Halifax a few weeks ago was not very satisfactory to members on th-is side of the House. I suppose he has received additional information with regard to the matter since that time.
I did not know anything about it then.

Our complaint was that on the occasion of the commitment to jail of a person who wrote an insulting letter in regard to the Legislature of Nova Scotia, some parties in Halifax hired the Royal military land, and that this band, the members of it attired in military uniforms and carrying military instruments, performed in connection with this incident. Objection was taken to this procedure in the province of Nova Scotia. I was very much surprised to find that irregularities of this kind are permitted by the Militia Department. It is certainly an improper thing to do. On former occasions serious objection was taken in this House to a military band parading in a religious procession. I see no objection to a band parading in a religious procession, but I do see very serious objections to a military band taking part in a procedure which constitutes an encouragement of lawlessness. The militia should stand behind the laws of Canada; that is what we pay them for. If the minister cannot enforce the will of Parliament he calls out the militia to do so, and it is certainly objectionable that they should be engaged in encouraging breaches of the law. I should like some better explanation from my hon. friend than he has already given.

The only explanation I
have to give is this: I had a good deal of trouble about these bands being permitted to turn out on some occasions and not on others. They were permitted to turn out on some religious, a good Orange demonstration for instance, or on the occasion of a political meeting, and in another case the services of the band were refused. It was decided, then, subject to the approval of the officer commanding the district, that the band might turn out for any legitimate purpose, providing they were paid for it.
Legitimate?

The question of legitimacy is determined not by us, but by the officer on the spot. The commanding officer at Halifax would decide the matter in this particular case. I made inquiries, and I found that there had been some trouble down there. A young man had been committed to jail and I understand that on the occasion in question they thought that he was coming out, but he did not come. The band, therefore, had to serenade him, I presume, and afterwards go home. My bon. friend's friends may want to use the band some time.
Not for such a purpose as that.

It might be; one can
never tell.

If it is open to any person to hire a military band to do anything at all, then it would be all right for the same people to hire the militia force of Halifax to pull down the jail and let Mr. McCurdy out. This man was committed to jail by order of the local legislature of the province of Nova Scotia and he should have been allowed to serve his sentence in peace without any military interference. If the minister thinks it is in order for a military band to take part in such matters, then it must also be in order for the militia itself to engage in them. I do not know where the minister will land himself if he announces a doctrine of that kind. If his commanding officer is responsible, I think he ought to be asked for an explanation. Has the minister received any such explanation?
Oh, yes.

Will he give it to the
committee?

It was given to the House some time ago. This band was hired by
the mayor of the city, if my memory serves me right, for the purposes of a procession. The officer commanding, because of the fact that a very reputable gentleman had approached him in the matter, thought that there was no harm in it.

That makes it all the
worse, if the mayor of the city had anything to do with it.

We had a case before this Parliament last year where a man named Miller was committed for contempt of this House. This Parliament, being a representative body of the King's authority, is just the same as the Parliament of the province, which is also representative of the King's authority. A man who is in contempt of this Parliament is in contempt of the King's authority; a man who is in contempt of the legislature of any province is in contempt of the King's authority as represented by the Lieutenant Governor. This man McCurdy was, in the judgment of that Legislature, representing the King and the Governor General, in contempt of the provincial parliament. We thought it proper last year to keep a man in jail during the whole of the session. This House thought that something like six weeks was a proper term of imprisonment. The Legislature of Nova Scotia dealt with this man very lightly and put him in jail for forty-eight hours only, the shortest sentence that could be thought commensurate with the offence. None of us would think it proper for one of the bands of the military authorities in Ottawa to be open to engagement by the people of Ottawa who might be admirers of Miller to go down to the jail of the county of Carleton and serenade Miller while he was in jail because he was in contempt of this House. The situation is exactly the same except that the King is represented by this Parliament is one King and the King as represented by the Legislature of Nova Scotia is apparently another. The Minister of Militia, representing the King and representing the King's authority, thought it proper to hire out the King's uniforms, the King's officers and the King's horses to go and serenade a man who was in jail because he was in contempt of the King's authority. Is that supposed to be consonant with what we should regard as proper decorum in matters of this kind? I am not talking politics but talking of the respect which we should hold for authority. The Minister of Militia must take it for granted that the judgment of the Legislature of Nova Scotia was right, that this

man was in contempt and was properly-imprisoned. Does he think it will advance the dignity of the institutions of this country to know that the King in one capacity is prepared to help put contempt on the King in another? The minister may take it lightly but we do not think the authority of the Crown should be held so lightly and contemptuously by a minister of the Crown as to hire the band or soldiers of any regiment, carrying the flag of our country, to go down in front of a jail and serenade and do honour to a man in jail because he is in contempt of one of the Legislatures of the province.

We knew nothing about the case until some days after it occurred. We have not yet received the final report of the officer in command of that district on the matter. As I understand this man was committed for a certain crime for forty-eight hours, but there was no warrant. That was found out, the jailer refused to retain him longer and the man could have walked out.
Mr. WM. CHISHOLM: Not at all, that is absurd.
He was confined regularly under the authority of the House.
I do not know, but I am told the sheriff told him he could go out and the man refused to go out because he thought that whatever omission there was in the papers would soon be inserted.
What had the band to do with that?
They were then going to give him this reception and he refused to take it.

That is not the case at all. The minister answered a question in the House sometime ago that this band was employed by a man named Bligh, who happens to be the mayor of Halifax. The band was employed to serenade or celebrate the release of this man who was imprisoned by the local legislature and the point made by the hon. member for Richmond when the matter was brought up was that that was not a proper use of the band. The minister said then that militia officers or men, including the band, were on duty when they were in uniform according to the regulations; these soldiers and bandsmen were in that sense on duty and they should not have taken part in this unlawful celebration. Has the $45 been paid that was promised for the use of the band on that occasion?

We have no record of
that, but we can inquire from the officer commanding at Halifax. It all rests with him.
Who is that officer who is responsible for this judgment?

The divisional officer
commanding, Colonel Rutherford.
Mr. WM. CHISHOLM: The minister has not answered whether he approves of the band showing contempt of the Legislature-

I could not express an
opinion until I know more about the ease.

Supposing that the
band went down and serenaded this man who was in gross contempt.

The hon. member will
.see that I would not care to turn around and censure Colonel Rutherford without knowing all the facts.

I am asking as a
matter of principle. Assuming the man was properly confined in jail for contempt. The facts were these: The man was committed to jail by order of the House. The Speaker directed the officer to take him to jail. The formal warrant was put in the jailer's hands some time afterwards. The procedure was similar to that followed in the magistrates' courts every day. The Order of the House was quite sufficient authority to detain him until the warrant was put into the proper officer's hands, so this man was in proper custody all that. time. If he had not been in proper custody proceedings would certainly have been taken to get him out under habeas corpus. Does the minister approve of any officer, speaking in the abstract, or would he attempt to justify any officer going to serenade, under the circumstances under which that band went in Halifax, a man in the position of McCurdy?
I am not inclined to express -any personal opinion at all.

I am sorry that my
friends from Nova Scotia do not know that there are two Kings in the country. There is the King whom we all, loyal citizens of Canada, revere and, by the speech which the hon. member for Perth delivered, I find that there is also King Carson. If the band went against the authority of King Carson then it would be very bad indeed.

The information we had was that not only did the band take part in this demonstration but soldiers in uniform marched at the head of the band carrying

the Union Jack along the streets of Halifax and that the band followed. I am surprised that the .minister cannot make up his mind about that question, that he hesitates to express any view about it.
The band could not parade without the flag.
That makes it all the more serious. The flag belongs to the regiment, and in this case was put to a most dishonourable use.
It has been used baaiy before.

It has quite frequently
been dragged in the mud by the Conservative party; but this is the worst case we have heard of for a long time. These soldiers, who are in the service of Canada, marched behind the Union Jack to the Halifax jail to serenade a man who had been incarcerated by the local legislature for making abusive statements reflecting upon that assembly. Surely the minister should not hesitate to say whether he approves of that kind of conduct or not. It will shock our faith in him as head of the military forces of Canada if he countenances anything like that. Assuming that this report is correct, that the soldiers at the request of some person joined with the mob and marched to Halifax jail behind the Union Jack, to show that the militia sympathised with the mob that was sympathising with this man who had been committed to jail for a serious offence, I think the minister should state whether or not he approves of that conduct on the part of his soldiers.
The hon. member has presented a hypothetical case.
No, it really happened.

I most certainly shall not condemn any of my officers until I know the details.
Mr. WM. CHISHOLM: It is quite apparent that the Minister of Militia is too patriotic a man to approve for one instant, of any such disrespect to the King as was shown on this occasion. He feels that in his heart of hearts, but, of course, there are certain reasons why he does not want to give expression to his opinion. Perhaps he feels that the boys down there were carried away by their political enthusiasm and stern devotion to the cause of Toryism, which, sometimes, is synonymous with rowdyism and ruffianism. I know the 316
Minister of Public Works approved of lawlessness of this kind on one occasion. A man who was being taken to jail at Moosejaw for crooked work at an election was rescued by a mob, and the Minister of Public Works spoke of these men as great patriots, men with blue blood in their veins, although they were guilty of a gross act of lawlessness. I know the Minister of Militia would not sympathize with any act of lawlessness of that kind, but at the same time he is a strong party man, and although he feels that this conduct on the part of his Conservative friends was most reprehensible, he does not like to condemn them. So I think under the circumstances we should excuse him from answering the question.

From Government

What does the Ross rifle cost, including rifle, bayonet and aperture sight?
The rifle costs $26.90, the bayonet $5, and the sight $1.10.
How much do you pay for a cannon?

It all depends upon
whether it is an eighteenrpounder or a thirteen-poundeT.	An eighteen-pounder
complete with guns, harness and so on costs iaJbout $45,000, that is, a battery of four guns.
How many such batteries are there at present?
About thirty-five.

Have you ordered any
Ross rifles lately?

I notice in the explanations given by the minister that the Ordnance Corps consists of fifty officers and 221 men, or a total of 271. That is given on page 12 of the memorandum, and
10 p.m. I notice that on page 11 the clothing for the new corps is to cost the country $200,000. There are only 221 men, and $200,000 seems a large amount for that very small force. It looks ias if the clothing of these men would cost $1,000 apiece. Surely that is paying more than is required for buttons and braid.

This is clothing for the new corps, not the Ordnance CoTps. This
[Mr. Lemieux. j
vote is for militia regiments*, batteries of artillery and regiments of cavalry and infantry. We have formed corps numbering ' some 7,000 men extra this year.
Under the head of ordnance?
We classify them in that way.
Why have you clothing in two places?

One item is lor the regular upkeep of the service and the other for new corps over and above the previous year.
Militia and Defence-Permanent force, $2,300,000.

What is the difference
between that and the other force?

Has the minister any
proposition to reduce the number of officers?

We have been increasing the instructional staff very materially in connection with the force. The force numbers 3,110 and it cost about $1,000 for each man in the service counting his pay, clothing, food and all that.
How many are there?
3,110. We are employing these instructors in connection with the cadet work.

A good many of these
officers are from the old country, are they not?
No, we are training, and giving positions to, as many of our home officers as we can.
Are men brought down from the old country to train them first?

Yes, they are brought
out.
But the majority of the officers are Canadians?
Yes, thiee to one.
What does the Ordnance Corps do?

We use the word 'ordnance ' in reference to artillery, etc., but the term ' Ordnance Corps ' applies to a corps that handles guns, stores and clothing. They have to look after clothing, amu-nition, rifles and that sort of thing and they are called the Ordnance Corps.

Why do we find so many officers looking after clothing and rifles? A few clever clerks Could do that kind of work. We have fifty officers and 221 men, or an officer for every four men. The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Borden), in his manifesto said that the militia force was top-heavy a few years ago, but the top has become a great deal heavier since my hon. friend took charge. He has increased the official staff enormously within the last two years.
No.

I have a return showing about fifty officers appointed to the corps within a year or two. There are fifty officers in the ordnance corps and 221 men, and if the duties of this corps are to hand out guns, ammunition and clothing, it looks to me as altogether indefensible that we should have one officer controlling four men doing that kind of work.

We found out that the
return that the hon. member speaks of included in the staff as well as the other officers in the force. There are a number of these officers who are instructors. It is very technical work.
Yes, but ordnance officers do not give instructions.

Yes they do. If my
hon. friend would go down and see these men the 'quartermaster general would show him what they do in half an hour.
Does the hon. gentleman say it is necessary to have one officer to every four men?

This is a corps that requires very few men, but it requires instructors of the highest class, and we have to have many of these men trained at Woolwich.
Royal Military college, $147,000.
What are the conditions attached to the Royal Military College?

A candidate for entrance has to pass an examination. These examinations are written in various parts of Canada. Wherever there are cadets who want to write we furnish an officer to conduct the examination. The minimum age is 16 or 17 and the maximum 21.

Where do the examinations take place?
316*
Wherever there are two or three candidates.

Have they to pay their own expenses while they are at college? There are some young men who go there who are what are called non-commissioned officers in the militia; are they not given a term of a couple of months free?

We have a course there for officers only. Non-commissioned officers would go possibly to the Kingston battery or artillery but officers not connected with the Royal Military College can go there and get a special course of instruction from the professors on the higher aspects of military work for two months or longer.
Is that free?
As far as the tuition is concerned.
Who is at the head of the Royal Military College?
Col. Carleton.

Where does he come
from?

He is a distinguished British officer of the Essex regiment.
.Militia and Defence-Salaries and wages,
For what?

This is for caretakers,
watchmen and firemen at drill halls and rifle ranges pay for messengers, clerks, labourers, etc. The pay is at the usual rate. *
Would the clerks have to pass the Civil Service examination.

No, they pass a military examination.
Militia and Defence-Schools of instruction $100,000.
Where are the classes of instruction?

We have classes of instruction wherever the corps are located- Kingston, Quebec, Halifax, etc., but in addition we furnish instructors at various centres wherever there are a number of officers, as for instance at Brockville. We send instructors to regimental and company headquarters. We send an instructor to any village or town where there are a dozen officers and non-commissioned officers who wish to take the course and an officer goes there to examine them.

Militia and Defence-Stores, $580,000.
Does that mean a reduction in the quantity of clothing and that kind of thing?

It means a reduction of the artillery outfit this year. We are cutting out something this year in order to keep the expenses down. At the time of the South African war the stores were practically depleted and my predecessor never caught up and we have never caught up with what we should have on hand.
What is included in the stores?
Saddlery, harness, tents, blankets, camp equipment, tools, bedding, artillery harness and all that sort of thing.

The minister told us
that all these goods were obtained by tender and contract; does he mean that tenders are publicly advertised for in the press? In a former discussion I received the same answer from the Minister of Public Works and from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries not very long ago, but I picked out at random some items in the Auditor General's Report, and I asked in what newspapers the tenders for them were advertised, and I was answered that they were not published in newspapers at all,' but that invitations were sent out to certain parties to tender. Apparently there are lists of favoured contractors in these departments who are asked to tender, and I suppose they are all of the one political stripe. Does the Minister of Militia purchase his supplies in the same way as these two other departments?

The same system is followed by me as was followed by my predecessor. These invitations are not sent all to Conservatives by any means. We have supplying us with goods, Mackenzie and Company, a good Liberal firm I believe, J. W. Woods and Company, and Workman of Montreal; they are still on the patronage list.
Yes, but do you call for tenders publicly?

We send circulars to
every firm the name of which is submitted to us as competent to do the work.

That is just what I
feared. I suppose those competent to do the work are always the political friends of the Government?
No.

Are tenders publicly
called for for the supply of boots?

No. We send circulars
to every boot manufacturer in the country.
Why do you not advertise publicly in the press?
If you did that you would have every newspaper from the Atlantic to the Pacific looking for the advertisement, and in the end it would cost more than the boots.
We never spent so much on newspaper advertising as now ?
Not in my department.

You will get ruled out of the Press Association.
Militia and Defence-Transport of freight, $200,000.

Does the Militia Department now send its troops over the Intercolonial railway or does it give its business to a competing company? I never could get the Militia Department to be fair to the Intercolonial railway; they seemed to want to send the troops over the Canadian Pacific railway or some other line, while the Intercolonial railway was struggling for existence. Has the minister got his officers converted to using the Intercolonial railway ?

I tied them up as tight as I could, but I wanted to know if they were now getting away ?
No, other things being equal, they go by the Intercolonial railway.
In a case of that kind the Government road ought to be patronized by another Government department, if anybody is going to patronize it.
We follow the Order in Council passed by hon. gentlemen.
Are the active militia, after their return from the annual drill, allowed to use their rifles at the ranges ?
Yes.

Are there rifles for
distribution among citizens for these ranges?
Yes.
Suppose, for example, I wanted to get rifles for those who wished to practise at the ranges, to whom should I apply?

Jf the hon. gentleman makes application on behalf of a company, the Quartermaster General will be sent down to inquire into it.
Militia and Defence-Training areas, $200,000.
Is Nabadogan one of these training areas?
Yes.	.
What is the policy of the minister in regard to these training areas, on which, I understand, a large amount of money is to be expended? What, for example, is the policy with reference to Nabadogan?
We know it by the name of McGivney Junction. There was an item last year by which an area was set apart there.

That is of some importance. What does the minister intend to use this training area for at McGivney Junction; does he intend to use it for the militia instead of the training areas in New Brunswick that were formerly used?

We had no training areas in the Maritime provinces; we had two small camp grounds, one at Kentville and one at Sussex; we are selecting these areas for the same purpose for which Petawawa is used, so that the troops will have an opportunity to manoeuvre. These other grounds are for smaller bodies of troops and rifle ranges, but they were quite inadequate for large movements.
That is very meagre information. What effect will this have on the present areas?

The cadet corps are
increasing, and the cadets now form a larger body than the militia formerly did. The cadets can go to the smaller areas and the militia to the larger areae.
It is practically wilderness land?
At the present time.
On whose recommendation was the place selected?

The New Brunswick
authorities were spoken to, and other parties.
What does the hon. gentleman mean by 'provincial authorities'?
Members of the provincial government.
They had the land for sale?
Yes. Four different areas were looked at.

Is it the intention to abandon the present camp grounds for New Brunswick and Nova Scotia and take the volunteer militia out to this wilderness and use that as a camp ground instead of Sussex and Kentville?
It is intended to use it for the purpose for which it was established. The other grounds are unsuited for the manoeuvring of troops.

I am afraid I shall have to disagree with the policy of the minister in this matter. I do this not alone because the present camp ground happens to be in my constituency, but because I think the whole thing is manifestly absurd from a militia point of view. As has been pointed out, there is difficulty now in getting men to go to camp; but if we are going to take men from all parts of the province and take them back to the woods where they will find nothing to fight but mosquitoes and black flies, and deprive them of communication with the civilized part of the country, you will find that your regiments will be reduced to mere skeletons -and in such a camp as is proposed your men will be reduced to mere skeletons anyhow. Is it the intention to move the camps at Niagara and other places in Ontario to the so-called training area at Petawawa? Or are New Brunswick and Nova Scotia to be singled out for special treatment in this matter? Now, take this camp at McGivney's Junction-
Excuse me-Nabadogan.

' A rose by any other
name would smell as sweet.'
It is not McGivney Junction.
East.

Settle your geography
some other time.
You know what the place is like?

I have a general idea. It is a tract of burnt woods and swamp. It is to be purchased, I understand, at $2 an acre. I do not blame the New Brunswick Government. They are wise to unload at a good price if they can on the somewhat credulous-along this line-Minister of Militia. They are getting $2 an acre or $200,000. It will cost at least $15 an acre to clear the land or $1,500,000. To erect the necessary buildings and carry on other works necessary to fit the place for the breeding of horses for cavalry will cost at least $300,000 or $400,000 more. So, this training area at McGivney Junction or Nabadogan will cost this country between $2,000,000 and $3,000,000.
The provincial Government has recommended it.

I do not want to disagree with what my hon. friend has said, but I think perhaps that is a misunderstanding-. The provincial Government would not have known anything about it had they not been approached by the Minister of Militia. Naturally they want to get rid of this land which is absolutely no use. It is Crown lands now but unfortunately it was visited by fire that rendered it useless for raising timber which was all it ever was good for.
The provincial Government are prudent in dealing with Crown lands anyway.
They have been since my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) left the Government.
Oh, oh.
That was a rather unfortunate remark from my hon. friend, in view of the history of Crown lands administration under his regime.
In this case they showed wisdom.

Yes. They sold land at $2 an acre that would not bring in the market twenty-five cents. So, I say, this is a wild, reckless and a foolish piece of extravagance, and I am opposed to it absolutely. I am opposed to it not on the sectional ground because it is proposed to take away the camp on one of the finest sites in Canada, Sussex-even historic

Niagara is no finer-but on general grounds. I regret that the minister still adheres to this policy: I had hoped that the arguments I have put forward would cause him to change his mind. Apparently he is determined as ever. This vote of $200,000-
It is not in this vote.
Then it was last year's vote, and that is dead.
It is last year's money, but still available.
How?
By Order in Council.
And not revoted? Is the purchase being made?
Yes.
Has the Order in Council been passed?
No.

Then, there is still a
chance.

It is amusing to any one who knows the difficulty of clearing land to hear my hon. friend the minister say that if you let a fire run through a forest, the land is perfectly clear. The very smallest part of the trouble and expense of clearing land is involved in touching a match to the timber and letting the fire run through it. The work to be done after the fire has covered the district is heavy and laborious, and if my hon. friend thinks that he is going to get troops, at fifty cents a day. to spend their time clearing black land, he reckons entirely without his host. It is difficult to get men at the highest wage to perform that service, because it is dirty, disagreeable work. To compare Sewell in the province of Manitoba, where there are prairie lands, with the forest backwoods of New Brunswick is a strange comparison for my hon. friend the minister to make. When he says that this land is worth $13 an acre and that the local Government are selling it at a sacrifice, $2 an acre, he talks very differently from the manner in which the Premier of New Brunswick talked when he returned from having a conference with my. hon. friend. He boasted and published reports in the newspapers about the splendid bargain he bad made for this worthless land at McGivney's Junction; that the Government were giving $200,000 for land which would not bring thirty cents an acre on the market.
With regard to the manoeuvring of troops, the man from behind the plough or behind the counter is given nine days in which to drill, because the days occupied in going and returning, as well as one Sunday are counted in. The hon. minister in these nine days proposes to have these
volunteers so taught that they shall be able to perform manoeuvres equal, I suppose, to the German or continental manoeuvres which he witnessed last year. I think that that is idle talk; at least, that is the way it seems to me. The plan hitherto adopted of drilling the troops and of teaching them the discipline of an army, of teaching them how to march and how to carry themselves, can be done in very much more restricted districts than 100,000 acres. I think that in many respects the hon. Minister of Militia is pursuing the right course in connection with his department, but I think that in this regard he is sadly astray and I trust that his colleagues who are here to-night will take note of what I say when the matter comes before Council, and that they will promptly turn down the proposal of the Minister of Militia to buy this tract which the generous and kind-hearted Government of New Brimewirk is so charitable as to offer him at the small sum of seven times more than it would bring in the market from any private person or firm.

At the present time we have to transport all the artillery from the Maritime provinces to Petawawa, and in this respect we will save in three years the entire cost of this maneuvring aTea and in five years the cost of clearing it.

I understand that the land in that district is very low and swampy. If the land selected is not dry, surely it would be unwise to use it. I understood the minister to say that the location is east of McGivney's junction; if it is, then my remarks do not apply. The portion of New Brunswick to which I have reference is west of McGivney's Junction.
We avoided that district; the range lies south of the National Transcontinental and east of the Canada Eastern.

The	Transcontinental
runs north and south.

The	Transcontinental
runs northwest and southeast. The area is east of the Canada Eastern.

The	Canada Eastern
runs east and west.
It is southeast of the Canada Eastern and southwest of the National Transcontinental.

I have seen a number of articles in the press of New Brunswick which state that this area is in the vicinity of Nabadogan junction, which is a divisional

point on the Transcontinental, twenty or thirty miles north of McGivney's Junction.
It touches the Nashwaak river and runs east.
Has the minister been on the tract himself ?
Yes.
Then the minister ought to know where it is. I understand him to say that it is west of the Transcontinental and south of the Canada Eastern.
The Transcontinental does not run north and south; it runs northwest and southeast.
The Transcontinental runs pretty well north and south. The tracks, then, would be south of the Canada Eastern and southwest of the Transcontinental.
It is between the Transcontinental and the river St. John, and between the Nashwaak river and the town of Sussex.

That is very definite; it is also east of Winnipeg. 'It is also somewhat west of Charlottetown, and it is north of the city of St. John and also west of Halifax. That location is about as accurate as I think the hon. gentleman is able to give us to-night. It does strike me as rather an extraordinary thing that the minister should have selected this site on the recommendation of the provincial Government, none of whom are military men except Cfolonel McLeod who was then a member. I would have supposed the minister, before deciding to abandon the splendidly located camp grounds at Sussex, would have had some recommendation from the officers of his department, by the commanding officer of New Brunswick, or of the Maritime provinces, recommending the minister to obtain a large area in this vicinity; but that he should have been induced to make the purchase upon the recommendation of the owners of the property is rather extraordinary. It is not usual to take that course, and it would rather look as if they were desirous of securing a good purchaser for the property.
In other words,, an easy mark.

They approached the minister and the minister acted on their recommendation. That is the statement we

have from the minister, that the recommendation was by the provincial authorities. The minister has also told us that by the provincial authorities he means the members of the provincial government who were the owners of the land. I have been at McGivney and at Nabadogan as well. It is certainly a most uninviting locality for a military ground. I am told it is true that the land is very low and requires a good deal of drainage. The members of the militia forces would be required to drain the land, and that would keep them pretty *well occupied for a long time before they could get it in such condition that it would be safe for horses to travel over. There is no doubt about that. In view of the very severe and, I think, just criticism which has been made against the proposed purchase by the hon. member who represents Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler), who, I believe, is himself a military man -I think he is an honorary colonel at all events-it seems to me that the minister, no matter how reckless he may be in other respects, no matter how much in harmony he may be with a reckless Government, in this matter, having been warned by his supporter, who has always been a zealous supporter of the Government, usually whether they are right or wrong, but whose conscience will not permit him to support this very great and unwarranted extravagance, should pause and prevent this transaction going through before it is too late. This is not a time when the Government can afford to waste $200,000. These are hard times for the Government and the people of this country. While $200,000 may not seem to be a large sum for hon. gentlemen in the Government, yet I am sure it will strike the members of this House and the people of this country generally that it is too large an amount to be wasted upon a tract of land which is not required for the purpose for which it is being bought, and which-and in this I quite agree with the hon. member for Kings and Albert-it would take a good many thousands of dollars, perhaps running up into the hundreds of thousands, to clear and drain and make suitable for the purpose of a camping ground.

I wish also to add my voice to the protest against any change of this kind in the Maritime provinces without very serious consideration. We have in Nova Scotia a very suitable plate for military manoeuvres at Aldershot. That is in the Annapolis valley, one of the most attrac-

tive parts of Nova Scotia; and I have no doubt it adds very much to the interest of the picnic the boys have when they go out to train, and that they are much more likely to go on a trip of that kind through the beautiful Annapolis valley than to go to a swamp in New Brunswick.
I object to the expression, ' a swamp in New Brunswick.'
I understand the proposal is to make this a camp for the Maritime provinces and to abandon the other camps in those provinces.

We do not intend to
abandon either Aldershot or Sussex.

Is this an additional
camp?

This is a manoeuvring
camp for New Brunswick and also an artillery range.
Is it intended that the other Maritime provinces shall have any share in the venture at all?

Prince Edward Island
will have a little area for their troops and Nova Scotia will have a suitable area.
Is it necessary to have 100,000 acres for military purposes?

I do not know where the hon. gentleman gets the idea of 100,000 acres. The area is 68,000 acres. I would ask the exMinister of Railways if he remembers what he paid for this land. He paid $13 an acre.

It is extraordinary that both one of the leading supporters of the Government from New Brunswick and leading gentlemen in the Opposition from the province condemn this proposal. If the minister has nothing more to say in justification than he has given so far I think it ought to be postponed.
Does the minister intend to take away from Aldershot camp in Kings county, .Nova Scotia, the training of the militia that has always has gone on there and to train them in New Brunswick?
There is no intention of taking the Nova Scotians to New Brunswick.
I understood it was for the Maritime provinces. Now it seems that Sussex is the only district to be affected; mine is the only one to be affected.
You are not affected.

You are reducing it from being a camp ground where the militia are trained to being a place for cadets to assemble two or three days a year. That does' not affect the general statement. I affirm that before this land can be made suitable for the manoeuvres my hon. friend speaks of, it will need to be drained as well as to be cleared and the draining and clearing will not be done by the volunteers. I have had a long experience in the militia of this country and from my experience I can say and affirm that volunteers going into camp will not do the work such as clearing and ditching while they are at camp. That work will have to be done and paid for, and even supposing the land is only 69,000 acres it will cost about $2,000,000 to get it ready for the purposes for which the minister claims it is to be used; but I think it is nearer 100,000 acres. That being the case, I think this expenditure is very unwise, unwarranted, and unnecessary, and that the scheme will not conduce to the benefit of the militia of New Brunswick.

As I happen to be the
only one in the House who happens to know anything about the land, I may say that it is neither flat nor wet; it i= sandy and rolling. A great deal has been cleared, and it Could be put in shape for the manoeuvres this season if necessary.

My hon. friend claims to have great knowledge of this land, but he was only there for two or three hours one day and I venture to say he did not see 500 acres of it. I was also invited to go with General Ian. Hamilton on that occasion, but as the place was very remote and the railway facilities very inadequate it was impossible for me to go.
The hon. gentleman does not know anything whatever about it. This matter has been discussed on former occasions.

Has the minister accurate information as to where the land is? From what I have been told by the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Loggie), and from what I have seen in the Government press I think this land is north and not south of the Canada Eastern.

If my hon. friend cares to come over I will show it to him on the map.
Militia and Defence-Contingencies-Amount required for medals, $6,000.
How many medals are to be given out?
These are in connection with the Fenian Raid. About $6,000 is required to purchase the medals.

Perhaps you had better not tell us what they cost each, or the veterans might not prize them so highly.
If we have disposed of the Main
11 p.m. Estimates, and the Supplement-aries for last year, I think we had better adjourn. We have done a pretty good night's business.

I want to get away to
Niagara camp if I can.

Is my hon. friend sure
where it is?
It is a little picnic ground at Niagara.
My hon. friend did not know the location of the camp in New Brunswick, and I thought he might have lost his bearings in Ontario.

I may say the New
Brunswick representative is not sure of it.
Militia and Defence-Amount required to reimburse militia corps amounts paid out by them for duty on uniforms imported, $25,000.
You are going to repay those who have paid duty?
That is the point.
Will you include my hon. friend from North Bruce (Mr. Clark) in this?
Yes.

My hon. friend raised
the point that officers' Uniforms should be admitted free of duty.
The Highland uniforms and the officers' uniforms are not made in Canada.

This is to reimburse
those who have already paid the duty?
No, to pay duty on the importation. I do not see how it can go beyond this year.
You had better make a limit or you will have to pay the duty for all past years.

No, it is for this year.
Militia and Defence-To complete Connaught Rifle Range-Further amount required $218 -
000.

This is going to be a
terrible affair before we get through with it.

No, $600,000, as I said at the outset, will nearly complete it.
Royal Military College-Further amount required, $7,600.
Why do you require an extra amount for that?

This is for the furnishing of the new dormitory.
Militia and Defence-Schools of instruction- Further amount required, $40,000.

I think the minister
ought to explain a number of these items in the Supplementaries.

This is for the instructional staff. We send officers to regimental and company headquarters all over the country to conduct classes. In many localities officers cannot leave home and take the course at the schools and so we send the instructors to the officers.

Did not the minister
have these instructors when the Main Estimates were made up? What I complain of is that the minister has been following the example of his colleagues; he has been trying to make the House and the country believe that great economy has been exercised in the Main Estimates because they have been a little less than they were last year, but that is more than made up in the Supplementary Estimates, and the result is that we have Estimates, main and supplementary, reaching the un-precedental amount of $17,000,000. The minister knew all these things when the Main Estimates were made up.

The number who are
making application for this course is much greater than we anticipated.
Militia and Defence-Petawawa-Amount required to pay claim Pembroke Dumber Company, $122,582.

Who is the Pembroke Lumber Company? This is a claim that has been up for a good many years, and I am told that the amount proposed to be paid is out of all reason and out of all proportion to the value.

I fought this off as long as I could. I have had a valuation made, the valuators being Mr. Rochester, of Ottawa; Mr. Campbell, a well known lumberman of the Ottawa valley, and a gentleman named Henderson, from my own county. Mr. Henderson's scale of measuring timber was different from the Ottawa valley scale, and he made the quantity less,
fMr. Graham..

while these two gentlemen made the figure a good deal more than he did.
Who are the Pembroke Lumber Company?
I think Mr. Dunlop i3 the president of it.
Yes, that is the milk in the cocoanut.
The hon. gentleman will certainly admit that my predecessor always recognized their claim, and kept a record every year of the timber that was cut?
Not for this amount.
I could not settle it in any other way.
What is the claim for?

For timber on this limit. This was a limit held by this company and at the time it was taken over the claim was not extinguished and the matter has been hanging fire ever since. They were offered $90,000 by my predecessor.

How many acres are
there?
It is fifteen miles square.

They had no freehold;
they only held a license from the Ontario Government.
No freehold.
Are they not getting an amount from the Ontario Government as well?
I am informed that they have to pay an amount to the Ontario Government for this license.

I have had a good deal of correspondence and information in regard to this matter and a lumberman possessing knowledge equal to that of any of these men whom the minister has named told me within the last three days that this was simply an outrage and that this property is an old second, third or fourth hand limit that was worked out years ago and has a little timber here and there and that they would have taken less than that amount of money from any person else and been mighty glad to get it. But one of the reasons why this amount is being paid is that Mr. Dunlop, the local member for North Renfrew, took charge of a certain campaign in South Renfrew and spent weeks at it at the instigation of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals. As
a consequence he had to get a mighty big price as a compensation for the labour performed, although that labour was useless. There is a good deal of talk among the lumbermen about how this company are imposing on the Dominion Government with reference to this particular piece of property. In the corridors of this building, within the last few days, one of the most prominent lumbermen in the country told me that it was an outrage. He believed that he could buy that property, if this thing had not come up, and that they would have been glad to have sold it, at the outside for one-third of what they are getting from the Government. That tallies with what the hon. member from Kings-Albert (Mr. Fowler) has said about the purchase of these other large areas of property. My information is, and I think it is correct, that this is simply-not a scandal, I do not want to put it that way because the minister has resorted to valuation-but it is simply an outrage that men can hold up the the Government, and it is very suspicious that the men who can do it are the men who have been so prominent in political work for several years.

When I heard of the claim for this I was astounded. I had only seen the northeastern part of the limit along the railway track, and I went up and traversed the entire limit, and I was more or less impressed with the fact that there is a good deal of good timber on it, but it is largely at the western side. I did not think it would be anything like this amount, and in order to get the thing down I got Mr. Rochester, who I understand is a leading Liberal in the city of Ottawa, and I deliberately picked him because he is a Liberal-
He is a Liberal all right.

Yes, he is a Liberal and jl picked him deliberately and he was recommended by a colleague in the Cabinet who wanted to have this thing done as squarely as it could possibly be done. I want to say that Mr. Perley went into the matter and said that Rochester should have an opportunity to see that there was not a dollar too much spent. Then there was Mr. Campbell, who I think is a Conservative, he is a member of the Quebec Legislature and one of the best-known lumbermen in the Ottawa Valley. I took a man from my own county, and I told him: I want you to watch with both eyes and keep this price down to the lowest possible limit, and his limit, as he admitted himself, was very low.
Was it not much lower than this ?

Yes, lower than this a good deal. When we consider that a few years ago my predecessor offered $90,000, and, as my hon. friend knows, every year's growth counts, and there are six or seven years since the $90,000 was offered-
But the Government has had the property.
That does not count; those lumbermen explained to me that the growth of timber counts.
Is it not our growth if we own the property ?
I must say that I thought the amount was very large, but I counted on Rochester holding it right down.
I understand it was not an arbitration ?
No.
These gentlemen were appointed arbitrators by the Government?
That is right.
That would be in order to justify it to the public if ever a complaint was made ?
It was to get at the value.
That is often done for the purpose I have mentioned.
That is an old trick of yours.
I usually instructed my engineers to value property. Did the minister have his own engineers value this property ?

I brought in a lumberman in my county who is one of the most prominent in the Dominion, and he valued it at from $60,000 to $70,000. We found afterwards that the maps furnished us did not include the whole area and that the most- valuable part of the. whole area was in a separate limit. When he valued that and put it all together it brought it up to considerably more but.it did not bring it up to this amount.

Did these gentlemen
take evidence?

My own man went over the limit and examined it tree after tree as far as he could, and then he averaged by the acre. These gentlemen spent weeks

measuring trees, and there are some amusing incidents as to the proper height to take a tree above the ground.
Did they make any report to the minister of the evidence of experts as to the quantity of lumber?,
They were all experts.
I presume the evidence would be in the department. In view of what the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has stated, I think the item ought to stand until we get that evidence?
They did not take evidence; they wrere supposed to be experts.

The minister says they
took evidence.
The evidence they took was that they measured tree after tree themselves, thousands of them.
Was there any statement showing the area and quantity of timber?
We have all the figures; my deputy will send them to the hon. gentlemen on Monday; I will not be here.
I will be glad to get it.
The claim they put in first was for $160,000, if I remember aright.

As I was from the eastern part of the province, I was waited on time and again as to the valuation of this timber at the Petawawa camp, before my hon. friend became Minister of Militia. If $90,000 wae offered it was offered as the extremest amount, and it was only offered then in order to get the thing settled up. I always made up my mind that they were asking two prices for the property, so far as I could make out.
I think about ten per cent more than it is worth.

A good deal more than that I think. I was watching for this settlement, and I feel confident that the Government has been done up to the extent of a great many thousands of dollars in connection with this property.
If my predecessor offered $90,000, and it is only $120,000 now after six years, we cannot be done up an awful lot.

It is thirty-three and one-third per cent more than the offer made

formerly, and that offer was the outside limit, and we all thought it was more than it was worth, but we wanted to get it settled.

The hon. gentleman
from South Renfrew was in the Ontario Government, and he knows well that licenses sold by the Ontario Government to-day are sold for three or four times more than they were sold for eight or nine years ago. These licenses are foT all time, and are not terminable as long as the holders pay the ground rent. The Ontario Government is buying back an area of the same limit from the same company for the Algonquin Park, and they are paying more proportionately for it than the Minister of Militia is paying for this property.

And if I were in the Ontario Legislature now I would have something to say about that. This gentleman, a good friend of mine personally, is a member of the Ontario Legislature, and he is getting a wonderful reward for his political work. He is getting an extraordinary price for this timber, and then a portion of it is to be bought back by the Ontario Government to go into the Algonquin Park at a higher figure, I think, than this Government has paid. If I were in the Ontario Legislature I would say the same thing as I am saying here, and perhaps with greater force.
Is not the hon. member mistaken in saying that the member for North Renfrew is the president of this company?
I do not know.
I think it is his brother.
It is a family affair; he is in it all right. If he were not in it this would not have been done either by the Ottawa Government or by the Ontario Government.
I know we all have our feeling in politics.
Not at all. The lumbermen are talking about it all over the district.

If my predecessor was
offered $90,000 a number of years ago, when the limits were not so costly or valuable as to-day, and considering the growth of timber since then, I do not think there is much fault to be found with this price. I am free to say I think it a little high, but I am not a judge. I counted on Mr. Rochester; I
never knew him before; but I said to Mr. Perley: 'I want a man that nothing can get round, a man that every one can swear by'. And he told me: 'Mr. Rochester is your man.' I understand Mr. Rochester is a leading Liberal; but he is a fair fellow. Then, Mr. Campbell is a man of absolute honour, a man who stands very high.
How many years is ,it since $90,000 was offered?
Six or seven years.
The minister took into consideration the fact that this Government must pay the Ontario Government for the freehold.
They took the property under the British North America Act, which gives authority to do so.

But the value of the
property must be paid to the Ontario Government.
We did not pay anything.

My hon. friend must be wrong. The Pembroke Lumber Company, have no vested right in this timber, but were simply licenses from year to year, and that fact would be taken into consideration in paying for the freehold. While it is customary for the Ontario Government to renew licenses, they were not bound to do so. The minister took that into consideration.
There was a case in my own county, where I thought I could get rid of a licensee, but I found that he had vested rights practically as in a freehold.

It depends upon the will of the Ontario Government. They could sell the land to settlers. But it is customary to renew the license, though not obligatory. I should think that this Government would have to pay the Ontario Government, if they have not done so, as owners of the fee, the value of the land and the timber as well.

That would not alter the case so far as this transaction is concerned from what it was when my predecessor offered $90,000. I am informed that interest was charged, although I did not know that before. But the Ontario Government would no more have to be settled with by us than by my predecessor.

I know the late Government refused to pay the Ontario Govern-

ment anything. They simply took the land, claiming the right to do so under a section of the British North America Act.
A section which allows them to take it for military purposes?
Yes, they took it and refused to pay for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With regard to the claim of the Ontario Government, when this settlement was made that Government agreed to limit any claim it might make to the dues it would have got under the lease had it been continued. This timber was worth to the Pembroke Lumber Company its value as it stood when we took over the land, but to get the timber they would have to pay dues to the Ontario Government. So they pay us the value of the timber, subject to a deduction for the dues they would have had to pay to get it, and the Ontario Government agree that as regards their timber claim they would limit it to the amount representing the value of the dues.
Progress reported.
